Project Outcomes Report

Over the past five years, the National Science Foundation’s Institute for Foundations of Machine Learning (IFML) has advanced the science and societal impact of artificial intelligence during a period of rapid global transformation. Established in 2020 and led by The University of Texas at Austin with major partners across nine other research institutions, IFML has worked at the nexus of foundational AI research, high-impact scientific applications, workforce development, and broadening access to computing education. Year Five marked a culmination of these efforts, with many IFML discoveries now deployed in widely used technologies and informing best practices across academia, industry, and medicine.

Advancing Foundational Knowledge in AI (Intellectual Merit)

A central outcome of the Institute has been major advances in the foundations of generative AI—models capable of creating text, images, biological molecules, and more. IFML researchers contributed breakthrough results across four key research areas:

Foundation Models. IFML teams developed new mathematical frameworks for understanding how large AI models generalize, how they can be adapted to new tasks, and how to prevent failures such as catastrophic forgetting. This includes new theory for zero-shot learning, improved methods for fine-tuning large models with minimal memory, and new approaches for stable self-training.

Algorithms and Optimization. IFML solved several longstanding open problems in optimization—the mathematical heart of machine learning. Researchers provided the first complete convergence guarantees for classical quasi-Newton methods, introduced new models for learning under distribution shift, and developed improved algorithms for differential privacy, reinforcement learning, and mixture-model estimation. These results advance the theory needed to train the next generation of AI systems more reliably and efficiently.

Diffusion Models. IFML played a leading role in the global diffusion-model revolution. Researchers pioneered Rectified Flow, now central to state-of-the-art image generators such as Stable Diffusion and Flux; created new methods for stylization and image editing now being deployed in Google’s Pixel devices; and developed inverse-problem solvers accelerating scientific imaging such as MRI.

Robustness and Safety. IFML produced new theory and algorithms for learning under contamination, detecting and responding to distribution shift, and building machine learning systems that provide certifiable guarantees. This includes the first formal model for testable learning under distribution shift and new frameworks for uncertainty estimation in streaming data environments.

Collectively, these outcomes have shaped modern understanding of how AI models learn, adapt, and fail—and have directly influenced both academic research trajectories and commercial model design.

Impact Through Use-Inspired Science (Broader Impacts)

Beyond foundational research, IFML translated its advances into high-impact applications in medicine, biology, scientific discovery, and open-source AI.

Medical Imaging. IFML models are now helping clinicians interpret echocardiograms automatically and accelerate MRI reconstruction. New algorithms have already entered clinical workflow, improving speed and diagnostic potential.

Generative Biology. Researchers developed new protein-design models that incorporate 3D structural information, yielding improvements over leading baselines. These tools are now being used with partners such as Houston Methodist and MD Anderson Cancer Center to engineer vaccine candidates and protein therapeutics.

AI for Mathematical Discovery. The Institute created new tools—such as PutnamBench—for training AI systems to solve and verify advanced mathematical problems, enabling progress in automated theorem proving.

Open-Source AI. IFML developed DataCompLM, now the largest public dataset for training language models, used extensively by Apple, AI2, and the wider open-source community. IFML researchers also contributed to OpenCLIP, a backbone of the global multimodal open-source ecosystem.

These projects have enabled progress in medical care, scientific research, and AI accessibility—areas where societal need is high and commercial incentives alone are insufficient.

Education, Workforce Development, and Broadening Participation

A major outcome of IFML has been transforming AI education at scale. The online Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence (MSAI) at UT Austin—launched through IFML—has expanded rapidly and will surpass 2,000 students in Fall 2025. Affordable tuition, flexible scheduling, and rigorous coursework have made advanced AI training accessible to an unprecedented population of working professionals. A new stackable graduate certificate now further broadens access.

Pre-college impacts include high-school AI summer academies reaching hundreds of students annually, K–12 curriculum modules used in more than 100 schools, and expanded summer programs at partner universities. Undergraduate research opportunities and large-scale matching events have connected hundreds of students with faculty mentors exploring interdisciplinary applications of AI.

Across all programs, IFML has broadened pathways into AI for students from schools lacking computing preparation, including more than 330 transfers through UT’s Accelerated Transfer Program.

A National Nexus for AI Research and Collaboration

IFML has functioned as a coordinating hub across academia, industry, and government. The Institute co-hosted major symposia on generative AI, deep learning theory, robotics, and computational science, regularly convening industry partners including Google, Microsoft, Amazon, NVIDIA, Meta, and Dell Technologies. These collaborations have resulted in production-grade deployments, high-impact open-source releases, and new multi-institution research programs such as ExpandAI.

abstractText:
This award is jointly supported by the Major Research Instrumentation, the Chemistry Research Instrumentation program, and the Chemical Measurement and Imaging program in the Division of Chemistry, and the Major Research Instrumentation in the Division of Materials Research.  With this award, Professors Sean Roberts and Carlos Baiz at the University of Texas Austin and Professor James Batteas at Texas A&M University are developing a sub-diffraction Time-resolved Super-resolution Microscope (TSM). This instrument enables measurement of dynamics unfolding over femtosecond-to-millisecond timescales with spatial resolution approaching 10 nanometers. The super resolution approach can be used to view fast processes such as electron motion in semiconductor nanostructures or dynamic restructuring of biological membranes. The TSM is designed to achieve three demanding needs, sub-diffraction spatial resolution, femtosecond time resolution and spectral resolution, from the near-UV to mid-IR. This can critically enable key insights into the inner workings of biological systems and creation of new materials for energy conversion and quantum information science. The microscope construction provides training of student researchers who work with the faculty.  After commissioning, the instrument is to be made available via its integration into the Center for Dynamics and Control of Materials (CDCM), a Materials Research Science and Engineering Center (MRSEC) based at the University of Texas at Austin. The project provides graduate students and postdoctoral researchers who use the instrument in their research the opportunity to develop a background in both ultrafast science and super-resolution microscopy.

The TSM is configured to employ laser pulses tunable from the near-UV to mid-IR to follow dynamics involving electronic, nuclear, and molecular motions.  An integrated atomic force microscope (AFM) allows in situ mapping of sample topography and near-field tip enhancement of signals produced in the region beneath the tip. The research enabled with the microscope will be directed by the principal investigators at studies of electronic dynamics at junctions formed between low-dimensional semiconductors and structural fluctuations within heterogeneous soft matter such as lipid membranes and polymer blends.  Other research directions to be explored with the new TSM instrument include energy and charge migration in solar energy materials, exciton dynamics in van der Waals heterostructures, energy and phonon conduction in thermoelectric and mid-IR photonic materials, ion migration in batteries and smart windows, biomolecule motion in cell membranes, nonequilibrium dynamics of photoactive polymers, and nanoscopic control of materials under intense electric fields.

projectOutComesReport:
Many materials and chemical systems are heterogeneous in their composition. For example, cell membranes contain several lipids, proteins, and other molecules whose spatial organization can be key to their function while materials used catalyze chemical reactions often feature nanoscale structures that act to improve their performance. Within these systems, important processes can unfold over a variety of timescales, from electron motion, which can occur over the course of a few femtoseconds (1 femtosecond = 1 millionth of a billionth of a second) to molecular diffusion, which can unfold over nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. As a result, developing tools that can resolve chemical processes at they occur in both space and time can enable new insights into how chemical systems function.

In this project, we have worked to address this challenge by creating a Time-resolved Super-resolution Microscope (TSM) that is capable of tracking dynamics within chemical systems with femtosecond-to-microsecond time resolution and a spatial resolution of a few tens of nanometers. This system functions by using an ultrashort pulse of light generated by a laser to initiate a chemical process and then using a second time-delayed probe pulse to measure changes that occur in a sample as a result of the chemical process. High spatial resolution is provided by coupling the light pulses to an atomic force microscope, an instrument that introduces a sharp metal tip to a sample surface. The metal tip acts to partially localize the light fields and as a result the signals measured from a sample report on chemical dynamics that occur near the tip’s apex. As the tip can be made as small as ~10 nm, this allows chemical dynamics to be read out from very small regions of a sample.

As proof of principle measurements, we have used the TSM to track energy migration within organic crystals that undergo a unique process known as singlet fission. Singlet fission is an energy conversion process that allows excited electrons in a material to share energy. This process can potentially be used to improve the performance of solar cells and photodetectors by reducing the amount of energy they dissipate as heat. Via measurements performed by the TSM, we have found singlet fission occurs at different rates within the bulk and at the surfaces of organic crystals. These different rates result from changes in how molecules are organized in these regions. By using the TSM to correlate molecular organization with function, we anticipate this work can inform the design of improved singlet fission materials that can meet demands needed for applications.

To make the TSM broadly available to the scientific community, we have incorporated it into an instrument facility operated by the Center for Dynamics and Control of Materials, a Materials Research Science and Engineering Center (MRSEC) supported by the National Science Foundation and located at the University of Texas at Austin.

abstractText:
This award will facilitate a variety of new activities by the University of Texas at Austin Groups and Dynamics (UTGD) research group. These activities are designed to foster a rich educational environment for undergraduates, graduate students, and postdocs at UT by increasing introductory research opportunities for undergraduates and research-level training for graduate students. The overall goals of this initiative are to increase the number of math majors going to top-tier graduate schools, increase the number of Ph.D.s obtaining top-tier postdocs, improve the career placement of postdoctoral fellows after their time at UT, and increase the number of women and minorities pursuing advanced degrees and careers in mathematics research and education.

The UTGD is led by seven faculty members at UT Austin. The group brings a wealth of different viewpoints and motivations together, from low-dimensional topology and geometry, to amenability, representation theory, random walks and ergodic theory. Building on a departmental Group Theory and Dynamics Seminar that has run for the past five years, the emphasis and resources of the grant will bring together expertise in the many areas represented by the research group while providing an arena for new mathematics and for the training of new mathematicians. To increase the number of graduate students entering into fields involving higher mathematics, UTGD will provide a summer Directed Reading Program (DRP) designed to prepare undergraduates for graduate school. UTGD will create a course, Experimental Mathematics, and enhance another, Discrete Math, to help prepare students for research. To improve the placement of graduating UT Ph.D.s, this award will enhance the UT graduate program by providing graduate fellowships/traineeships and travel funds and support for graduate mini-Schools and a Groups and Dynamics junior seminar. To build the departmental activity centered around Groups and Dynamics, this award will add four postdoctoral positions and provide visitors to work with postdocs, graduate students, and faculty. In the use of these resources, the management team will actively seek to increase the proportion of members of underrepresented groups in mathematics. The grant also proposes a number of ways to impact mathematics outside the department. The materials resulting from any of the projects will be made available through a dedicated website. The mini-Schools will draw from graduate students nationwide; the undergraduate  conference, and the summer DRP will draw broadly from Texas schools. The Julia Robinson Math Festival will bring engaging and new mathematical experiences to K-12 students in the Austin area. The activities with the Math Teachers' Circle will create a stronger working relationship between the faculty and students of the math department and local K-12 teachers.

abstractText:
Optical tweezers won the 2018 Nobel Prize in physics for their applications in biological systems. The tweezers use a highly focused laser beam to trap and manipulate small objects, including cells, particles, bacteria, and virus. Despite the huge success of optical tweezers, the requirement of sophisticated optical setups and high working power prevent their non-invasive manipulation of fragile objects. Tremendous efforts have been made to develop new techniques for optical trapping. However, a universal strategy to safely manipulate different particles and cells in various liquid environments is still elusive. This proposal aims to develop a new optical tweezing platform based on laser cooling and thermal migration of particles in a temperature gradient. Laser cooling can create a localized cold spot on a substrate where various particles can be trapped by thermophoresis. The cooling-induced trapping is expected to effectively avoid the thermal damages due to optical heating in conventional optical tweezer, and the general thermophoretic migration behavior allows this strategy to be used for a wide range of biological cells and nanoparticles to advance life sciences and biomedical applications, including tissue engineering, cellular biology, early disease diagnosis, and drug delivery. The proposed research at the interfaces of physics, photonics, thermo-fluidics, colloidal sciences, and biology will provide interdisciplinary research opportunities for graduate students, undergraduate students, and K-12 students. The outreach efforts will be integrated into two existing Women in Engineering Program initiatives on campus to increase recruiting women and underrepresented minorities into engineering. 

Opto-thermophoretic tweezers were recently developed as an alternative strategy to manipulate particles and cells in a light-controlled temperature gradient with simple optics and low operation power. However, the current laser-heating-based opto-thermophoretic tweezers suffer from limited applicability to special solvent conditions and potential optothermal damages. The objective of this proposal is to develop and apply new opto-thermophoretic tweezers based on laser cooling of the substrates. Due to the common thermophobia in colloidal species, a variety of biological cells and particles can be trapped at the laser beams via thermophoresis in their native environments. In addition, this design can avoid thermal damages due to the temperature increase in optical tweezers and the heating-based opto-thermophoretic tweezers. The proposed research will provide a novel platform for versatile and non-invasive optical manipulation for nanoparticles and biological cells. The intellectual merit is that the proposed research will improve fundamental understanding of laser cooling and thermophoresis, establish safe optical manipulation techniques for cells in biological media, and advance biological applications of optical tweezers, including studies of cell-cell interactions and thermal cues in cellular behaviors.

projectOutComesReport:
Traditional optical tweezers rely on high laser power and refractive index contrast, often causing thermal and photon damage to trapped objects like biological cells and nanoparticles. While optothermal tweezers offer reduced laser power requirements, they remain limited by medium constraints and excessive laser heating. To address these challenges, the NSF-funded project on Laser-Cooling-Driven Opto-Thermophoretic Tweezers (LCOTTs) aimed to enhance precision, versatility, and biocompatibility in optical manipulation, contributing significantly to advancements in the laser manipulation field. Key goals included investigating the transport of colloidal particles in laser-cooling-induced temperature gradients, developing LCOTTs for thermophoretic trapping, and demonstrating dynamic manipulation of cells in biological media.
Progress and Key Achievements
2020-2021: Foundational Research and Platform Development
During the first year, foundational work established principles of laser-cooling-driven optothermal manipulation. The team developed LCOTTs using Ytterbium-doped Yttrium Lithium Fluoride substrates, achieving multimodal manipulation, including out-of-plane rotation of micro-objects. These advancements laid the groundwork for the integration of thermophoretic effects with laser cooling, reducing power requirements and improving trapping precision.
2021-2022: Expanded Capabilities with Optothermoelectric Tweezers
Building on initial progress, the project demonstrated the potential of optothermoelectric tweezers by integrating polyethylene glycol (PEG) and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solutions with functionalized substrates. This system harnessed synergistic light-induced depletion forces, thermoelectric effects, and electrokinetic forces to achieve safe and effective manipulation of nano- and micro-particles. Notably, yeast cells were manipulated through safe tweeze-and-roll operations, demonstrating biocompatibility and utility for biomedical research.
2022-2023: Breakthroughs in Three-Dimensional Manipulation
The project achieved significant advancements in three-dimensional manipulation of plasmonic vesicles using Hypothermal Opto-Thermophoretic Tweezers (HOTTs). This approach enabled controlled cargo release for potential drug delivery applications while minimizing thermal damage and power usage. Additionally, the team developed a multimodal manipulation system for navigating rough biological surfaces, overcoming substrate limitations.
A novel single-cell rotation-based method was introduced for high-resolution, label-free quantification of subcellular binding kinetics, enhancing understanding of cell adhesion dynamics. These developments underscored the versatility of optothermal techniques for biomedical and biophysical applications.
2023-2024: Advanced Applications and Multicellular Organism Manipulation
The final year of the project focused on expanding the scope of LCOTTs to address more complex scientific challenges:
  1. Thermophoretic Behavior in Coacervate Droplets
    The team explored thermophoretic behaviors in heat-dissociative coacervate droplets, uncovering how temperature gradients drive molecular redistribution and interfacial tension variations. These findings provided insights into prebiotic molecular organization, contributing to the understanding of the origins of life.
  2. Microrobotic Swarms with Adaptive Navigation
    Adaptive algorithms were developed to enhance responsiveness and stability in LCOTT-based microrobotic swarms. Through real-time feedback control and an elliptical-approximation algorithm, long-distance autonomous navigation of microrobotic swarms was achieved, including obstacle avoidance in constrained environments.
  3. Multicellular Organism Manipulation
    The project extended the optothermal manipulation platform to C. elegans, integrating laser-generated microbubbles with cooling systems to enable biocompatible manipulation. The Marangoni convection flow and surface tension of the bubbles facilitated dynamic chemotaxis assays, showcasing the system's potential for broader biological research with minimal damage to the nematodes.
Broader Impacts
The project's outcomes highlight transformative potential for optothermal manipulation across a wide range of fields. Applications span from precision drug delivery to autonomous microrobotics and fundamental biological studies, offering novel tools for biomedical, biophysical, and nanotechnological research. Furthermore, the project contributed to workforce development by training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in cutting-edge optical manipulation technologies.

title: Laser-Cooling-Driven Opto-Thermophoretic Tweezers

abstractText:
The rate of star formation peaked when the Universe was 3 billion years old. Curiously, when you look back even further in time, when the Universe was only 1-2 billion years old, some galaxies have seemingly already completed their growth, becoming very massive, with little ongoing star formation. Finkelstein and his team will use data from the Spitzer/Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment Exploratory Large Area (SHELA) survey to discover and catalog 5000-10,000 massive galaxies and quantify how many are quiescent. To investigate why these galaxies had such a short and effective growth spurt the team will make a detailed comparison to simulations, deciphering which combination of physical processes reproduce the observations. A cohort of undergraduate students will be paired with graduate students to form the first Vertically Integrated Project Team at UT Austin. Secondary school teachers will attend a residential workshop at McDonald Observatory, resulting in ~4,500 students learning about this research through classroom activities during this 3-year project. 

The 23 square degree SHELA survey consists of optical imaging from the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory/Dark Energy Camera (5-sigma depths of ugriz=25-26.5 AB mag; Y=22), near-infrared imaging from the Kitt Peak National Observatory Mayall 4 m Telescope/National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory’s  Extremely Wide-Field Infrared Imager (K=23) and the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy (J=21.3, K=20.9), mid-infrared imaging from Spitzer/Infrared Array Camera ([3.6], [4.5]= 22.3 mag), as well as coverage in the X-rays from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and sub-millimeter from the Herschel Space Observatory.  Finkelstein and his team will leverage this order of magnitude increase in sample size to  i) publish a multi-wavelength photometric catalog of massive  (log M/Msol > 11) galaxies at 3<z<5, robust against both Poisson and cosmic variance; ii) measure the quiescent fraction as a function of stellar mass and redshift; iii) perform a critical analysis of contamination rates in the quiescent galaxy sample using spectroscopic observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array and the Keck/Multi-Object Spectrometer For Infra-Red Exploration, and iv) compare the data to multiple theoretical simulations to explore which simulation best matches the observations.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Massive galaxies (10-100X more massive than our Milky Way) in the early universe are excellent laboratories of the most extreme processes which shape star formation.  While in today’s universe nearly all massive galaxies are quiescent (showing little ongoing star-formation activity), it was previously shown that the opposite is true in the early universe.  At what epoch due massive galaxies quench their star-formation, and which physical processes are responsible?  The frontier is now at redshifts greater than 3 (a few billion years after the Big Bang).  Modern simulations predict that massive galaxies should be entirely star-forming at this epoch, but there were hints from previous work that this was not the case.  However, such observational efforts were hampered by small volumes probed, leading to small numbers of rare, massive galaxies, making conclusions difficult.

Our work centered around constraining the abundance of massive quiescent galaxies at a time 1-2 billion years after the Big Bang using data from the Spitzer/HETDEX Exploratory Large Area (SHELA) survey, a new legacy imaging survey covering 27 square degrees. During the first part of this award, we focused on creating a new photometric catalog in this field, making use of the abundance of new ground-based imaging data.  This “infrastructure” work led to the creating of a catalog spanning 16 photometric filters, containing an amazing four million galaxies.  During this time, we also tested selection techniques for massive, quiescent early galaxies, using ALMA millimeter data to rule out contamination from dusty more nearby galaxies.  We found that with our catalog we can robustly select massive quiescent galaxies, with a contamination rate of only ~10%.

During the last portion of this award, we focused on selecting a sample of the most extreme galaxies, identifying a sample of 20 bright, massive quiescent galaxies at redshifts greater than four.  We have secured spectroscopic followup with the Gemini telescope, with data coming in soon.  We expect these data to confirm many of these sources, which will provide the strongest observational evidence that early galaxies are able to grow to exceptionally large masses, then quench their star formation, all within less than one billion years.  Such processes are not predicted by simulations, thus new physical processes must be implemented.  

Our primary broader impact was the expansion of our Galaxy Evolution Vertically Integrated Projects (GEVIP) undergraduate research program. This is an immersive, multi-year research program that involves sophomores through seniors, with returning students gaining valuable peer-mentoring experience bringing younger students up to speed. Following the induction of our Fall 2024 cohort, our team now includes 17 undergraduates. In summer 2023 we also ran a teacher workshop funded by this grant, where ~a dozen secondary school teachers went to McDonald Observatory.

title: The Onset of Star-Formation Quenching in Massive Galaxies in the Early Universe

abstractText:
It is now well established that our universe is undergoing an accelerated expansion. The initial observations in the late 1990s for this expansion come from observations of distant Supernova and have held up to latest analysis today. It is not known what causes this acceleration, named “dark energy”. It is believed to be responsible for about 70% of the matter energy density of the universe. There are many theories  for the cause of “dark energy”: perhaps new particles, vacuum energy pushing the universe outward, modifying the theory of relativity concerning the laws of gravity, or some other unknown process which will lead to a more detailed understanding of the evolution of the universe from its  origin in a “Big Bang” to the present day.  The Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment (HETDEX) will collect data on at least 700,000 galaxies that are 9 to 11 billion light years away allowing astronomers to measure how fast the universe was expanding at different times in its history. Changes in the expansion rate will reveal the role of “dark energy” at different epochs which will be used to validate/negate the predictions of various theories or give new clues that will lead to a final solution. The observational program for HETDEX is fully funded, and currently about 25% complete. This grant will support the compilation of a detailed catalog containing the calibrated data products that will be available to the scientific community and the public for additional astrophysical science studies. A cell phone app will be developed for a Citizen science program using the data products.

This grant will amplify the science from HETDEX by combining a vetted catalog with a public database that will be employed for ancillary science by the scientific community and citizen science applications. The neural networks used for the spectral extractions for classifying the galaxies in the catalog to meet the HETDEX specifications need to be optimized.  Partial support will be for an expert at the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) to  design the public access to the data base including web development, and data base maintenance and will interface with the postdoctoral fellow for vetting the catalog for the optimization of the visual classification into machine learning. The information from the classification campaign will be folded back into the reduction software for continued reduction optimization.  This will allow the data base to be maintained and updated for subsequent data releases as more about the system is learned.  This support will build a truly useful data base for the internal use of the HETDEX program, public access for additional science the scientific community as well as Citizen science projects using the cell phone application that will be developed for this program.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
HETDEX is a major experiment to understand the expansion of the universe as it was 11 billion years ago. The overall goal is to determine the nature of dark energy. We have obtained 0.7 billion spectra over 7 years of observations. The data collecting is complete. This database is the largest spectral catalog ever obtained, and it will all be public. We are in the process of generating the sources that we use from the spectra. These galaxies are undergoing significant star formation in the early universe and we find them by their emission in the transition of Lyman-alpha. We currenty have 1.5 million of these galaxies cataloged and are in the process of determining the real sources from false positives. In order to help with false detections, we are using the public through the Dark Energy Explorers (DEE). This site has already reached over 13k volunteers and generated over 2.5 million classifications. The results from DEE are being used in machine learning efforts to make a clean sample of sources. The other major ongoing endeavor is to calibrate each of the individual 6000 fields observed. The variety of observing conditions and variations in the instrumentation requires us to run extensive simulations. We have reached specification for the number of sources and expect to reach percent level measures of the expansion rate of the universe 11 billion years ago. Matached with other ongoing surveys, the lever arm provided by HETDEX will give unique understanding of the nature of dark energy.

abstractText:
With this award, the Macromolecular, Supramolecular and Nanochemistry Program in the Division of Chemistry is funding Professor Nathaniel Lynd of the Department of Chemistry at the University of Texas at Austin to develop new polymerization techniques for the controlled synthesis of polyethers.  Polyethers are a class of large molecules in which every repeating unit contains a carbon-oxygen bond.  They are typically prepared from small cyclic carbon-oxygen containing compounds called epoxides.  This class of polymers is becoming increasingly important in today’s society because they are easier to degrade pathways than widely used plastics that contain mostly carbon-carbon bonds along the main polymer chains.  Hence, polyethers might provide a viable solution to the recyclability problem which is of vital importance from an environmental perspective.  In this research, catalysts based on aluminum are systematically designed to speed up the synthesis.  The new chemical reactions are simple and can be transferred to laboratories around the world, which could greatly expand access to these types of polymers.  This research is having a broader impact by providing education and research training to a diverse population of undergraduate and graduate students.  Additional outreach efforts are focused on interactions with students from the Austin School for the Deaf and K-8 students through on-campus introductions to polymer chemistry at the Introduce a Girl to Engineering Day at the University of Texas-Austin. 
 
This research is focused on development of Lewis pair catalyst systems for functional polyether synthesis.  There is currently no consensus polymerization technique available for polyethers that provides access to polymers with controlled molecular weights, chain-end functionality, good tolerance to monomer functionality, and availability to the non-specialist.  This research seeks to further the development of such a tool by exploring the kinetics and mechanisms of the N-Al Lewis pair catalysts.  Steric and electronic factors that govern Lewis-pair catalyst activity for epoxide polymerization are systematically explored.  Detailed studies associated with Lewis pair formation and structure are also conducted.  Special emphasis is placed on the investigation and elimination of parasitic initiation/termination through decomposition of a zwitterionic intermediate resulting in alkyl, or hydride terminal polymers, and/or undesirable cyclization.  The methodology associated with this work introduces a readily available polymerization platform requiring only mixing of two commercially available chemicals.  As such, it opens doors to new chemists with limited technical or infrastructural means to convert structurally diverse epoxides into functional and useful polymers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
This project seeks to apply a Big Data approach, harnessing emerging standards for paleoclimate data, to address two fundamental questions in climate dynamics: (Q1) the spatial extent of abrupt changes in hydroclimate; and (Q2) How can knowledge of past temperature variations help reduce the spread of twenty-first century climate projections. The potential Broader Impacts include building capacity in Big Data analysis in the global paleoclimate community. All analyses will be shared as open-source computational narratives to disseminate best practices in paleo data science among early-career researchers, and to provide a template for future analyses of this kind.

Specifically, the researchers will leverage recent paleoclimate data synthesis efforts, as well as advances in the analysis of chronologically uncertain timeseries, to explore fundamental questions in Holocene paleoclimatology. The proposed work will also link paleoclimate data to future climate projections from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) ensemble.  The project will provide training to early career scientists through three yearly workshops in data management and analysis based on workflows and methodology developed as part of this research. Additionally, the project will support one graduate student working at the intersection between paleoclimatology, data science, and climate modeling. Other Broader Impacts include outreach through the Young Researchers program and Center for Knowledge-Powered Interdisciplinary Data Science to expose high-school students and graduate students in data science to interdisciplinary research.

projectOutComesReport:
The goals of this project were to 1) teach new researchers how to employ mathematical techniques and software packages (i.e. ‘Big Data’ approaches) on climate datasets via a “Hackathon” and 2) use similar techniques to learn about past climate changes. For Goal #1, we held four Hackathons sessions in Feb 2021, Oct. 2021, and Mar. 2022, Jun. 2023 servicing ~200 scientists from around the world, including many from the United States. In these sessions, the program language Python was heavily utilized as a tool for the ‘Big Data’ calculations. These workshops help to teach proper statistical techniques to young scientists, and the software packages in Python created by and disseminated during the Hackathons aid to standardize calculations across the field.

 

For Goal #2, we developed a new technique called Laplacian Eigenmaps for Recurrence Matrices, or LERM, to analyze the underlying changes in climate time series. We then use this technique, along with other mathematical tools, to analyze the so-called 4.2 ka event that was used to demarcate ‘The Meghalayan Age’, which serves as a Global Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP). We use stalagmite reconstructions from the SISAL Version 3 database to analyze the 4.2 ka event, as stalagmite records from the region have the best resolution and age uncertainty to constrain short climate events – especially over land. We show that this event was not even synchronous regionally across Southeast Asia, and therefore not a global event, as regional changes are a required first step in showing that an event is global. This result invalidates the event as a GSSP and usage of The Meghalayan Age as geologic age.

abstractText:
The Macromolecular, Supramolecular, and Nanochemistry Program in the Chemistry Division supports Professor Sean T. Roberts at the University of Texas at Austin to study light-triggered processes that occur in materials.  Light provides the energy that fuels plant growth via photosynthesis, is used in electronics for wireless communication, and even forms the basis for noninvasive medical treatments, such as photodynamic therapy used to treat cancer. However, light transmits its energy in a peculiar manner, via particles known as photons. Different colors of light contain photons with different amounts of energy, and it is important that photon energies be matched to their intended applications. Photons with too little energy are unable to meet their intended task while photons with too much energy waste energy and can cause damage to components. This research project develops materials that reshape light’s energy content by combining pairs of photons into a single high-energy one or converting individual photons into multiple lower-energy photons. Once formed, these materials can serve as energy transfer agents improving solar energy harvesting and quantum computation. In addition to working with students closely on the research projects, Professor Roberts also founded and participates in the GReen Energy At Texas (GREAT) program, which was formed between the University of Texas at Austin and Austin Community College.  GREAT aims to increase the number of community college student that earn degrees through targeted mentorship and research experiences.

Semiconductor quantum dots chemically functionalized with organic dye molecules offer an ideal interface for photon conversion. Quantum dots energized by light absorption can pass their energy to molecules at their surface, promoting them into spin-triplet exciton states. If formed in high quantity, pairs of spin-triplet excitons can undergo triplet fusion, a process that combines their energy to form a single high-energy spin-singlet state that can radiate light. Likewise, photoexciting the dye molecules can fuel triplet fusion’s inverse process, singlet fission, which creates pairs of triplet excitons that can each pass to the quantum dot to drive infrared light emission. These schemes require a key step, the transfer of a spin-triplet exciton across the quantum dot:molecule interface, yet an understanding of how the structure of these interfaces impacts the rate and efficiency of spin-triplet exciton transfer is elusive. To address this need, Professor Roberts at the University of Texas at Austin directs a team that employs controlled chemical synthesis, 2D NMR and femtosecond time-resolved spectroscopies, and electronic structure calculations. The research team investigates how the chemical structure of quantum dot:molecule interfaces formed by two complementary quantum dot materials of PbS and Si impact spin-triplet exciton transfer. This project contributes to the creation of new hybrid organic:inorganic junctions for light-driven production of energy and fuels as well as materials that use spin entanglement for quantum computation and information storage.

projectOutComesReport:
Due to its ability to transmit energy and information through space, light plays a central role in nearly all aspects of human society. However, light has a peculiar property as its energy content is transmitted by photons, discrete particles whose energy must be matched to their intended application. Materials that reshape light, by combining the energy of multiple low-energy photons to generate high-energy photons (photon upconversion) or by using single high-energy photons to produce multiple low-energy ones (downconversion), can enable new light-driven technologies and optoelectronics.

In this project we designed hybrid structures comprised of inorganic quantum dots interfaced with organic ligands that capture light and use its energy to drive either photon upconversion or downconversion. Quantum dots are small nanocrystals whose light absorbing and emitting properties depend on their size while ligands are molecules that bind (ligate) to their surface. Light absorbed by a quantum dot can excite its electrons, whose energy can be passed to ligands at their surface. These ligands in turn can act as antennas for funneling energy to molecules in the surrounding environment. This can place these molecules into a particular type of excited state, known as a spin-triplet state, that can be long-lived on molecular timescales, lasting for hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds. Pairs of molecules in these long-lived states can collide and pool their energy together, deexciting one molecule while promoting the other into a high-energy state that can emit light, providing a means for achieving photon upconversion. In principle, this scheme can operate in reverse to drive downconversion.

However, for this light conversion approach to operate efficiently, energy must be able to readily transfer between quantum dots and ligands bound to their surface. To achieve this goal, we have performed studies aimed at understanding how the chemical structure of the interface formed by molecular ligands and quantum dots controls their ability to exchange energy. For our studies, we focused on three types of quantum dots comprised of different compounds that absorb and emit distinct colors of light: PbS (near-infrared), Silicon (green/red), and CsPbBr3 (blue).

In a set of studies, we found the rate of light-induced electron transfer PbS quantum dots to perylenediimide (PDI) electron accepting ligands could be controlled by altering the conformation adopted by these ligands on the quantum dots’ surfaces. By either introducing “spectator ligands” that cause PDIs to bend towards the PbS surface or reducing PDI aggregation that restricts their ability to bend towards the PbS surface, we could accelerate electron transfer. As electron transfer is related to energy transfer, design concepts from our work for structuring the ligand shell of PbS quantum dots can likewise be applied to speed energy transfer for photon upconversion.

In silicon quantum dots, we found energy can move back and forth along covalent silicon-carbon linkages formed between the dots and ligands anchored to their surface over nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. This ability to exchange energy in different directions suggests silicon quantum dots can readily be used for both upconversion and downconversion. Importantly, by controlling the structure of covalent silicon-carbon links between quantum dots and ligands, we can push them into a strong coupling regime wherein photoexcited electrons are simultaneously shared between a dot and each ligand bound to its surface. Such states generate unique opportunities for moving energy between a dot and its environment as all ligands bound to a dot can potentially act as an energy donor following light absorption. In related work, we have found similar strongly coupled states can be formed in solid arrays of CdSe quantum dots through proper choice of surface ligands and act to accelerate energy diffusion through the array.

Lastly, we have examined how the chemical structure of the bridging group used to affix ligands to blue-absorbing CsPbBr3 quantum dots impacts their ability to fuel blue-to-UV photon upconversion. By binding naphthalene-based energy acceptors to CsPbBr3 dots via carboxylate linkers rather than amines and optimizing linker placement on acceptors, we can significantly speed energy transfer. This improved performance results from several factors, including stronger binding of carboxylates over amines to CsPbBr3 and stronger electronic coupling between naphthalene and CsPbBr3 facilitated by carboxylates.

In addition to our scientific results, we have worked to expand the STEM workforce via Connecting Research and Education A TExas (CREATE), a program that introduces community college students to modern STEM research through research seminars and a summer internship program. During this project, nearly forty students at Austin Community College completed research internships focused on areas related to chemistry and nanoscience at UT Austin. This project also developed a research-focused classroom exercise that can be integrated into organic chemistry courses to introduce students to research in a classroom environment. This exercise has been piloted by students at Austin Community College, who have successfully created a library of novel diketofurofuran dyes for applications in photon upconversion and downconversion.

abstractText:
The way bilinguals and monolingual elders speak an endangered indigenous language is not uniform. Bilinguals are typically more dominant in one of their two languages, in most cases not their indigenous one but the national or dominant language in their country of origin. Monolingual speakers differ from bilinguals in having one single, fully developed, linguistic system. This difference can be seen in their use of words, especially complex verbs, since a range of semantic nuances that are idiosyncratic to their speech are displayed. The speech of elderly monolinguals in indigenous languages is vanishing as villages decrease in population, leading to significant losses of cultural diversity. 

In this dissertation project, the doctoral student will document naturalistic spoken monolingual speech and provide an in-depth analysis of the grammar and the semantics of verbal morphology in a particular monolingual variety that will allow answering questions such as: What is the  verbal morphology of elderly monolinguals like and what grammar underlies such complex systems? What semantic information is prominently displayed through the verbs used by monolinguals that is not present in bilingual speech? These questions remain just loosely explored in current literature. The results of this project will enhance understanding of the diversity of endangered indigenous languages as it brings into the analysis monolingual systems which are morphologically more elaborate, thus allowing researchers to evaluate different cross-linguistic theories of morphologically complex languages. Since the doctoral student is bilingual, data collection will include her participation in everyday conversations. This interactive process will guarantee gathering real speech while spontaneously interacting with elderly monolinguals. Complementary elicited data will also be gathered to help achieve a better understanding of the semantics of verbal morphology. The naturalistic data corpus collected will be transcribed, annotated and analyzed, and will then be curated and deposited in a digital archive for the use of a wide range of stakeholders including indigenous language speakers, linguists, and other researchers.

projectOutComesReport:
This grant allowed the co-PI to conduct documentation of a variety of South Bolivian Quechua (SBQ) spoken in a rural town in Southern Bolivia. The co-PI recorded a fifty-hour linguistic corpus in audio and video while interacting solely in SBQ with elderly monolingual speakers. This documentation allowed the co-PI to produce a doctoral dissertation titled: Verbal complexity in South Bolivian Quechua: insights from the speech of monolingual elders’. The dissertation describes the complexity of verb forms found in the SBQ variety spoken in the rural town of Uma Piwra. This variety is only spoken by elders and had not been documented. The co-PI also produced two academic papers, ‘Constituency and word formation in South Bolivian Quechua’ (in press) and ‘Associated Motion and Direction in South Bolivian Quechua’ (submitted)

The co-PI produced the first large naturalistic corpus of SBQ, consisting of 50 hours of the recordings with linked transcription and translation, to be archived at the Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America (AILLA). The documentation also facilitated the production of a community-oriented book. In addition, the co-PI wrote and published a comic book !T’akayacharikamushallanñataq! ‘The rain is starting to fall downwards again’ The book highlights how humor is preserved in the speech of monolingual elders in rural towns and promotes public awareness about the endangerment of the linguistic and cultural diversity of South Bolivian Quechua that is maintained in rural towns.

Finally, concerning the impact in the Bolivian society, this research project trained a group of SBQ-speaking younger students to document monolingual varieties in different towns in Southern Bolivia. As a result, two of them managed to enter grad school in the United States.

abstractText:
The importance of the numerical simulation of physical phenomena by computers cannot be overstated. Such computations have become essential tools both in scientific research and in industrial research and development. This project concerns the numerical simulation of the scattering of waves. Such simulations have applications to sonar and radar, as well as in medical imaging, geophysics, and many other applications. Wave phenomena become more complicated to model as the frequency of the wave increases, and our current ability to accurately model high-frequency waves is quite limited. This project seeks to develop new methods for modeling high-frequency waves efficiently and to high accuracy. The project provides research training opportunities for graduate students. 

The numerical simulation of the scattering of waves from inhomogeneous media has important applications in radar and sonar, medical imaging, geophysics, and a host of other scientific applications. In many cases of interest, such simulations can be performed by solving the variable coefficient Helmholtz equation. The solutions of this equation are oscillatory, and the difficulty of calculating them using conventional approaches grows quickly with the frequency of the oscillations. Recently, one of the investigators developed a new class of solvers for the variable coefficient Helmholtz equation that achieve extremely high accuracy and have run times that scale much more slowly with increasing frequency than conventional solvers. They operate by solving the nonlinear Riccati equation that is satisfied by the logarithms of solutions of the Helmholtz equation. Currently, these solvers only apply in special cases. This project aims to extend them to the general case to develop a method for the variable coefficient Helmholtz equation that is significantly faster than current techniques.

projectOutComesReport:
The numerical simulation of the scattering of waves from inhomogeneous media is a central building block of modern scientific computing. This problem lies at the heart of mathematical modeling of medical imaging, geophysics, non destructive testing, and a host of other applications. In many cases of interest, such simulations can be performed by solving a mathematical equation known as the "variable coefficient Helmholtz equation". The solutions of this equation are oscillatory, and the difficulty of calculating them using conventional approaches grows quickly with the frequency of the oscillations. Indeed, in the high-frequency regime, when the solutions of the variable coefficient Helmholtz equation oscillate rapidly, conventional approaches become prohibitively expensive.

The project supported the development of several new techniques that make computational modeling of wave phenomena faster and more accurate. Of particular note is a new solver that was developed in collaboration with doctoral student Anna Yesypenko. This technique is designed for wave propagation problems in heterogeneous media, and is engineered to take full advantage of modern computing hardware. It parallelizes well, and fully exploits GPU accelerators. The solver has been implemented for problems in both two and three dimensions, and has enabled the solution of problems that were previously impossible to solve without the use of super computers.

Another discovery concerns a set of numerical techniques for converting a class of continuum equations that model scattering phenomena into large systems of linear equations that can be solved using computers. The new technique was discovered by combining insights from differential geometry with mathematical results concerning so called "lattice sums". It was proven that the dominant terms in the errors incurred when a continuum surface is locally approximated by polynomials can in some cases be evaluated exactly, and expressed in terms of derivatives of the Riemann and Epstein zeta functions. The ideas were implemented in code and tested on realistic geometries in two and three dimensions. These methods proved to be substantially faster and more accurate than previously existing methods.

The project supported the professional development of several early career STEM researchers. Two doctoral students were directly supported with research assistantships, and the research supported facilitated the training of several other students and postdocs. During the course of the award, two doctoral students involved in the work graduated, and one more will graduate shortly. Three postdoctoral scholars involved in the work have secured tenure-track assistant professorships at research universities.

abstractText:
Cave organisms as unrelated as insects and salamanders often have shared features – such as lack of eyes, pallid coloration, and elongated limbs. Life underground provides different challenges from life on the surface, and those challenges favor relatively rapid changes in appearance (and other, more subtle characteristics) at the population level. Those rapid changes lead to convergence in the appearance of many cave organisms, but the genetic and developmental processes that lead to repeated changes in different organisms are largely unknown. The Edwards Plateau of central Texas has an extensive, though fragmented, network of springs, caves, and aquifers that host numerous, diverse, underground salamanders. These salamanders attain reproductive maturity while retaining features (such as gills) that are characteristic of immature salamanders, and many of them show eyes reduced in size and development to varying degrees, along with other characteristics associated with living underground (e.g. an enhanced sense of smell).  These characteristics have evolved independently and repeatedly in the various species, and this research will integrate information derived through a variety of approaches to shed light on the mechanisms that enable new structures and functions to evolve. This project is timely because in addition to enhancing understanding of the evolution of sensory systems, it will highlight and clarify the diversity of salamanders in central Texas at a time when human population growth and commercial development further threaten species that have been identified as being in danger of extinction. Finally, this project will serve as a platform to train numerous undergraduates in STEM research.

The researchers will use an integrative, hierarchical approach combining genetic, developmental, and phylogenetic perspectives to study the mechanisms that drive convergence in phenotypes of subterranean Groundwater Salamanders. Results from micro-computed tomography imaging, histology, transcriptomics, and exon sequencing will demonstrate the degree of morphological convergence in sensory systems (visual, olfactory, and lateral line) across subterranean lineages. Comparative transcriptomics will be employed to examine the developmental genetic mechanisms of organ system reduction and signatures of molecular convergence at the protein-coding level in sensory-system genes.

This project investigated the developmental and genetic mechanisms driving phenotypic convergence in groundwater salamanders (Eurycea), a remarkable radiation endemic to the Edwards Plateau of central Texas. This work provides key insights into repeated evolutionary processes in subterranean environments by integrating comparative developmental genetics, phylogenetics, and morphological analyses.

Intellectual Merit

This study improves our understanding of the processes responsible for repeated evolution by (i) investigating the extent to which phenotypic convergence is mirrored by molecular convergence and (ii) characterizing the developmental genetic basis of derived similarity. Results have shed light on how and through which pathways new structures and functions can evolve. Finally, this project exemplifies integrative biology by combining approaches from different subfields within a comparative, hierarchical framework, including:

  • Morphological Analyses: Micro-computed tomography (microCT) and histology quantified the degree of convergence in sensory systems (visual, chemosensory and mechanosensory) across subterranean lineages. Eye development showed common early stages, diverging significantly later, alongside compensatory enhancements in mechanosensory organs.
  • Comparative Immunohistochemistry: We discovered that the PAX6 protein, known for its role in eye development, is also present in the lateral line system of Eurycea salamanders, where it is concentrated in the hair-like tips of sensory cells. This suggests a previously unknown role for PAX6 in cell structure and movement, expanding its known functions beyond vision.
  • Molecular Convergence: Using transcriptomes from multiple populations of all species in this group, we are testing for selection at the protein-coding level, asking whether morphological convergence reflects parallel molecular evolution.

Results demonstrated the hierarchical nature of convergence—occurring at morphological, developmental, and genetic levels—and highlighted the interplay between relaxed and heightened selection pressures in subterranean habitats. The reduction of visual systems in subterranean environments is compensated by an increase in mechanoreception via an increase in the number of neuromasts of the lateral line system. These compensatory changes have evolved repeatedly in multiple invasions of subterranean environments. These findings advance our understanding of how similar traits arise independently, shedding light on evolutionary and developmental pathways that shape biodiversity.

Broader Impacts

This project had significant impacts on education, diversity, and public engagement, particularly in STEM retention for underrepresented groups:

  1. STEM Education and Inclusion:
    • Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience (CURE): The project contributed to UT Austin’s Freshman Research Initiative (FRI), a nationally recognized program integrating authentic research into undergraduate education. Through the “Biodiversity Discovery” research stream, students gained hands-on experience in molecular biology, bioinformatics, and morphological analysis. The FRI program is proven to increase STEM retention rates by 23%, with 50% of participants from underrepresented minority (URM) backgrounds.
    • Summer Research Exchange: A collaborative summer program between UT Austin (Carnegie R1 and a Hispanic-serving institution) and Texas State University (a Hispanic-serving institution) trained more than 25 summer undergraduates. Students gained interdisciplinary skills, working on microscopy, developmental genetics, and computational analyses while developing independent projects. This initiative addressed barriers faced by first-generation and URM students, fostering retention and career readiness.
  2. Mentorship and Career Development: Annual research meetings brought together undergraduates, graduate students, and faculty to present findings and receive constructive feedback. These meetings provided professional development opportunities and platforms for scientific communication, boosting student confidence and skills.
  3. Community Engagement and Conservation: The iconic Eurycea salamanders, celebrated locally in Austin and San Marcos as symbols of conservation, were an effective focus for public outreach. Educational initiatives targeted K-12 students, using interactive tools like 3D-printed salamander models to inspire interest in biodiversity. Public lectures and media coverage emphasized the importance of groundwater ecosystems, connecting the project’s research to broader conservation goals.

Conclusion

This project demonstrated how integrative research across genetics, development, and morphology can uncover the processes driving convergent evolution. Beyond advancing basic science, it provided a robust STEM education and training framework, thereby improving the retention of diverse groups of science students. By combining rigorous research with impactful outreach, this work supports scientific discovery and the development of a skilled, inclusive STEM workforce.

Non-Technical Description:
The Texas Nanofabrication Facility (TNF) will enable research and development in nanoscience and technology, with applications in nanoelectronics/photonics, green energy and healthcare. TNF will provide state-of-the-art capability in nanodevice prototyping, metrology, and nanomanufacturing. This will include, for example, research in nanosensors for the Internet-of-Things, high efficiency solar cells for green energy, and nano drug delivery systems. TNF is the only NNCI node in the southwest region of the US, encompassing Texas and the neighboring states of Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana. The efforts in prototyping of nanoelectronic devices in the cleanroom will be enabled by training of users by NNCI staff, as well as by staff providing remote services for external users who are unable to travel to TNF. Coupled with device fabrication, TNF will provide cutting-edge tools in nanoscale imaging and metrology at the atomic scale. Located in a vibrant US technology hub in central Texas, TNF will have tremendous impact in nanotechnology education and entrepreneurship, particularly among under-represented minorities such as Hispanics, a sizeable minority in Texas, and Native Americans in Oklahoma. Furthermore, TNF will perform social scientific research to explore the ethical implications of nanotechnology. We will regularly host tours of our cleanroom, research facilities and nanotech labs, and host popular lectures on nanotechnology for K-gray members of the public because education and outreach are critical to creating an informed public, and securing the economic and environmental future of the US.

Technical Description:
The Texas Nanofabrication Facility (TNF) at the University of Texas at Austin (UT-Austin) is composed of the Microelectronics Research Center (MRC), the Texas Materials Institute (TMI), and nanomanufacturing fab (nm-Fab) which collectively house over 130 major tools in 22,000 sq.ft. of labs, staffed by 25 professionals. The MRC cleanroom provides extensive nanofabrication capabilities, TMI provides state-of-the-art metrology tools, while the nm-Fab developes and provides novel nanomanufacturing tools in the areas of roll-to-roll manufacturing, and high speed, large area nanoimprinting. Our vision is to continue to enable and foster breakthrough nano-innovation in the areas of electronics and energy, which have significant presence in the South West. TNF will partner with the new Dell Medical Hospital at UT in the area of healthcare electronics and nanomedicine. Specifically, TNF will focus on science-to-scalability, where one integrates nanodevice prototyping with nanodevice manufacturing for industry. TNF will foster an innovation ecosystem by connecting our industrial users to the Longhorn Startup undergraduate entrepreneurship course at UT-Austin, the Austin Technology Incubator, and NSF I-Corps program. TNF will establish educational activities in nanotechnology directed at engaging underrepresented minorities, particularly Hispanics, who are a sizable minority in Texas, and women. Under the REU initiative, the facility will partner with Austin Community College to provide year-round research and training experience in nanotechnology for two-year college students.  Furthermore, TNF will explore the social and ethical implications of nanotechnology, and start a new effort on Education/Outreach focused on Computation and NSF Quantum Leap.

Intellectual Merit

The Texas Nanofabrication Facility (TNF) at the University of Texas at Austin (UT) is composed of the Microelectronics Research Center (MRC) which has been part of the NSF NNIN program since 2004, the Texas Materials Institute (TMI), and nanomanufacturing fab (nm-Fab). NNCI-TNF (composed of MRC, TMI and nm-Fab facilities) has 22,000 sq. ft. cleanroom space (class 100 and 1000) and 20,000 sq. ft. of labs. We partner with Austin Community College (ACC). The MRC cleanroom provides extensive nanofabrication capabilities, TMI provides state-of-the-art metrology tools, while the nm-Fab has developed and provides novel nanomanufacturing tools in the areas of roll-to-roll manufacturing (deposition and etch), and high speed, large area nanoimprinting. TNF is well positioned geographically in the Austin high-tech hub, within the Dallas/Fort Worth-Houston-San Antonio triangle, with no competing universities having comparable infrastructure in nanotechnology in this region of the country.  

Broader Impact

 Since Texas, in general, and Austin in particular, have a strong industry base in nanotechnology, TNF has a large external user cohort, especially in terms of small companies. We also serve academic institutions in Texas, and the neighboring states. We also have users from other parts of the US, and the rest of the world. We have enabled and fostered breakthrough nano-innovation in the areas of electronics, healthcare and energy – all of which have significant presence in the SouthWest. Through NNIN/NNCI, UT supported 600 users/year with 70 industry users.

Publications

The NINN/NNCI grants resulted in over 1,000 publications over 10 years, including high impact journals such as Science, Nature, PRL and Nano Letters.

abstractText:
The Southern Hemisphere westerly winds are a crucial component of the global climate system, playing an important role in controlling the weather of the Southern Hemisphere mid-latitudes through the seasonal transmission of precipitation-generating storm systems, as well as through their influence on the circulation of the Southern Ocean. It has been hypothesized that past changes in the position and strength of the westerlies may have also impacted the global carbon cycle through their influence on storage of carbon dioxide in the deep ocean, with impacts on global climate.  Models also suggest that future warming will also result in changes in the westerlies, with the potential to drive changes in the storage or release of carbon dioxide from the Southern Ocean. However, the westerlies respond to a number of factors including regional, hemispheric and global patterns of warming, ocean circulation and Southern Ocean sea ice cover.  In order to better understand how these factors influence the westerlies and their potential role in changing in the carbon cycle, this research project will generate a new reconstruction of the westerly wind response to a range of natural climate factors over the past ~140,000 years. In combination with the results of climate model simulations, the results of this study will provide a better understanding of how and why the westerlies change, and will thus provide a perspective from the geological past on how the westerlies will respond to future changes in global climate. The impacts of this research on society will be presented to the public through venues such the University of Texas Geoforce program, local community organizations, ongoing activities and outreach at local K-12 schools, through programs such as Girls Start and the Boy Scouts. 

This research will focus on the generation of a new high-resolution record of past westerly wind behavior using the laminated sediment record from Lake Orakei, a volcanic crater lake located on the North Island of New Zealand.  Reconstructions will use the hydrogen isotope composition of sedimentary leaf waxes as a proxy for the position of the westerlies, an approach that is grounded in a study of modern isotope dynamics in this region. The reconstructions will be complemented by temperature reconstructions based on the MBT’5ME paleotemperature proxy and will focus on understanding the timing and nature of the westerly response to orbital forcing, the growth and retreat of the ice sheets and, over targeted intervals, the response to millennial-scale variability during Dansgaard-Oeschger and Heinrich stadials.  A robust proxy-model comparison approach will be used to better understand the underlying climate dynamics driving the westerly wind response to these forcing mechanisms.  This award is cofunded by the Division of Earth Sciences and the Division of Atmospheric and Geospace Sciences by way of the Paleo Perspectives on Climate Change Program.

projectOutComesReport:
The Southern Hemisphere westerlies are a critical component of the climate system, playing an essential role in connecting climate changes between the hemispheres through changes in atmospheric circulation patterns, ocean-atmosphere interactions and the carbon cycle.  At the same time, the past history of the westerlies, and the climate of the Southern Hemisphere mid latitudes in general, is poorly constrained by existing geological reconstructions – leading to numerous and conflicting interpretations of past changes in the westerlies, and their response to changes in the climate system.  

The goal of this project was to generate new reconstructions of past changes in the westerlies and hydroclimate using new paleoclimate reconstructions from the North Island of New Zealand.  To do so, we used lacustrine sediment records from Lake Pupuke (0-40 kyr BP) and Orakei Basin (~30-140 kyr bP), which together provide a continuous record of the last glacial cycle in the mid latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere.  Temperature was reconstructed using the MBT’5ME index, which is an empirically derived paleotemperature proxy based on structural variations in bacterial membrane lipids preserved in the lake sediment records. The position of the westerlies was reconstructed using the hydrogen isotope composition of sedimentary leaf waxes (long chain n-alkanes), which are interpreted as a proxy for the stable isotopic composition of precipitation. Data from modern isotope sampling suggests that precipitation isotopes reflect changes in moisture source related to the seasonal north-south migration of the westerlies. The reconstructions from New Zealand were supplemented by additional Holocene lake records from SE Australia. 

            Our reconstruction of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies from Lake Pupuke is strongly correlated with changes in the Intertropical Convergence Zone, likely as a consequence of changes in the Hadley circulation.  Northward shifts of the ITCZ are associated with equatorward shifts of the westerlies on millennial to orbital timescales.  These shifts are consistent with previously hypothesized associations between changes in the position of the westerlies and atmospheric CO2- related to wind driven ventilation of the Southern Ocean.  Simulations using fully coupled Earth system models show responses consistent with our reconstructions during both the Holocene and in response to millennial-scale climate shifts.  However, during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), our reconstruction suggests the westerlies shifted poleward, in disagreement with theory suggesting an equatorward shift in the westerlies that was responsible for a reduction in Southern Ocean ventilation. However, our result is consistent with some model simulations suggesting that the expansion of sea ice may drive local southward shifts of the westerlies during the LGM.  On longer timescales, our reconstruction shows significant variability on obliquity timescales, which we hypothesize may be due to the influence of changes in the Earth’s tilt on high latitude seasonal sea ice formation.

            Our reconstructions also suggest that changes in the westerlies and temperature are decoupled.  Temperature variability, particularly over the last ~40,000 years, is strongly correlated with high latitude temperatures reconstructed from Antarctica – showing similar orbital to millennial scale variations. Thus, at least in some regions high latitude temperature changes extended into the subtropical mid-latitudes. Changes in temperature – particularly during the deglaciation -are also strongly correlating with the timing of past glacial retreat – suggesting that mid latitude glacial systems responded most strongly to temperature, not precipitation.

            Together, these data provide unique insights into long term climate variability in the Southern Hemisphere mid-latitudes.  They suggest that climate variability in this region reflects the complex interplay between local hemispheric forcings and changes in the high latitudes of both hemispheres.  The data support a potential role of the westerlies in ventilation of the southern hemisphere and changes in CO2 on some timescales, but suggest that the response is complex and likely varies over time and with changing boundary conditions. However, it also provides valuable targets for future investigations with better constraints on factors like Southern Ocean sea ice cover, ocean circulation and the connections between mid and low latitude circulation systems.

This project involved training of two Ph.D. students at the University of Texas, Austin. In addition, this project also involved collaboration with scientists in New Zealand and Australia.  PhD students had the opportunity to conduct research internationally and work directly with students and researchers at these institutions. Both PhD students also had opportunities to engage in educational and outreach opportunities including involvement in the University of Texas GEOFORCE program, which encourages students at the secondary school level to get involved in STEM fields and the University of Texas RTX summer research program, which offers opportunities for undergraduates to get involved in an immersive summer research and training program.

abstractText:
The scientific study of signed languages has provided insights into the human capacity for language and differences between spoken and signed modalities. Studies reveal that all human languages change over time—regardless of modality. There is a large body of generalizations about spoken language change, which are typically framed as relevant for human language generally. However, the vast majority of the proposed general features of human language change were developed without consideration of signed languages. In spoken language, the sounds that combine to form words often change in regular and systematic ways over time, and these regular sound changes form the empirical basis for language families. Signed languages have units that combine to form signs, but no research has been done to clarify whether regular sound change has a correlate in signed languages, or if regular language change is unique to spoken languages. This project will be the first to rigorously explore this question. It will also provide research experience to several undergraduates and professional development to a postdoctoral associate.


The three-year project will investigate linguistic change and relationships among 13 signed languages. It will develop a database of signs for 207 basic concepts in each language, drawing on online and print dictionaries. Deaf native signers of the languages will check the signs and provide missing entries. Each sign will be transcribed to allow both manual and automated comparisons of the signs’ phonological units across all languages. The dataset will then be evaluated using two methodologies: the traditional Comparative Method (CM), and network-based and Bayesian phylogenetic approaches. If the CM yields evidence of regular and recurring correspondences, the researchers will identify cognates and reconstruct earlier stages of the languages. Lack of such correspondences will provide evidence that some aspect of signed languages either inhibits or disguises the regular changes on which the CM depends. Quantitative phylogenetic approaches are complementary to the CM because they do not depend on regular change to assess patterns of similarity among languages.
