projectOutComesReport:
The overall goal of this project is to develop mechanistic understanding of coupled seasonal hydrologic and chemical processes in coastal sediment and aquifers above permafrost. We evaluated two main ideas:

(1)  The dominant mechanisms and pathways for supra-permafrost groundwater flow across the land-lagoon and benthic sediment-lagoon interfaces, or ‘submarine groundwater discharge’ (SGD), change seasonally through lagoon ice break-up, the open-water and maximum thaw period, and through freeze-up and over-wintering. And,

(2)  As the groundwater flow regimes change seasonally, so do the quantity and quality of organic matter and inorganic nutrients delivered to the lagoons by groundwater.

The study quantified terrestrial and marine groundwater fluxes and investigated the underlying flow and transport processes needed to understand how the mechanisms, quantities, and chemical characteristics of groundwater inputs to Arctic coastal lagoons varied seasonally. This study involved field work during spring (lagoon ice break-up and shallow active layer on land), late summer (lagoon open water and deep active layer), and fall (freeze-up), and included computational flow and transport modeling informed by extensive observations. Machine learning was employed to develop further predictive insight.

Our team, which included a total of 3 PIs, 1 postdoctoral fellow, 1 technician, and 7 graduate students (UT Austin – 4 PhDs and 1 MS; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution – 1 PhD and 1 MS), conducted field work at Simpson Lagoon near Deadhorse/Prudhoe Bay, Alaska four times (August 2021, and June, July, and September 2022). The team employed geophysical techniques, conventional hydrogeologic characterization, measured natural radiogenic isotope tracers onshore and offshore, and conducted computational groundwater flow and transport models. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) and inorganic nutrient concentrations, DOM compositional indictors, and DOM lability, and trace metal concentrations were measured in groundwater, coastal water, and river water collected during different seasons.  The geochemical data were used in combination with the water discharge estimates to calculate fluxes of DOM, metals including mercury, and nutrients.

The intellectual impact of the project includes the following discoveries:

(1) Hydrologic measurements and radiogenic tracers indicate high rates of SGD.

(2) Using a Ra mass balance model, we found that the SGD water flux was substantial and dependent on environmental conditions. No measurable SGD was detected during the spring sampling period (June 2022), when the lagoon was partially ice-covered. During ice-free periods, the main driver of SGD is wind-driven lagoon water level changes, not tides, which control surface water recirculation through sediments along the lagoon boundary.

(3) Groundwater contained an order of magnitude more dissolved organic carbon (DOC) than rivers, with average concentrations increasing from break-up to freeze-up. Groundwater contained three times or more biodegradable DOC (BDOC) than rivers. Groundwater DOM is highly aromatic yet biodegradable and thus may be an important energy source to Arctic coastal waters in summer when river inputs are low.

(4) A multi-year seasonal study of total (THg) and methyl mercury (MeHg) inputs to Simpson lagoon showed that SGD inputs of THg during spring are negligible, while during summer and autumn they are no greater than inputs from rivers. However, SGD inputs of MeHg far exceed riverine and other inputs to the lagoon during ice-free periods in summer and in autumn, indicating that groundwater could be the dominant source of Hg bioaccumulation into the coastal food web and for the people who rely on marine fish and mammals for sustenance.

(5) Through integration of observations and process-based models, we found that regardless of ice-bonded permafrost depth at the shore, summer SGD flow dynamics along portions of the Beaufort Sea coast of Alaska are similar to those in lower latitudes. Calculated summer FSGD fluxes in the Arctic are generally higher relative to low latitudes. The FSGD organic carbon and nitrogen fluxes are likely larger than summer riverine input. The FSGD also has very high CO2 making it a potentially significant source of inorganic carbon.

The results have been published in 3 peer-reviewed journals. 3 more manuscripts are under-review, and 3 more are being written up or revised.

The broader impacts include:

(1) Transfer of knowledge through conference presentations (at least 20).

(2) Training of graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. All graduate students directly supported by the project have graduated, and this includes 2 PhD students and an MS student at UT Austin and 1 PhD student and an MS student at WHOI.

This project showed that SGD happens in the Arctic at rates and through processes that are not too different to lower-latitude regions. It is the first project to show this through integration of direct observations and less direct observations via tracers. It also quantified the fluxes of both organic and inorganic compounds, both of which are important for the ecology and water quality of the coastal waters. This knowledge provides important baseline knowledge as the Arctic coastal areas undergo profound changes with global warming.

abstractText:
Modern control systems supporting today’s critical infrastructure (e.g., transportation network, power systems) are comprised of a large number of computational devices interconnected over communication networks. Such systems are commonly called Networked Control Systems (NCSs), and have been the subject of research interest over the last two decades, both from theoretical and practical perspectives. The maturation of technologies in both wireless and wired communication made various NCS concepts realizable (e.g., connected cars, remote surgery, cloud-based control), and the roles of NCSs will further grow in the future. Recently, however, the advancements of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasing demand for AI-powered control algorithm implementations over NCS architectures. While these new trends exemplify the remarkable capabilities of NCSs, they raise unprecedented challenges to the current form of NCS technologies in terms of: (1) capacity to incorporate Big Data contents that support emerging AI-based control schemes, (2) scalability to accommodate a large number of players within limited network resources, and (3) security against and privacy from potential adversaries. 

The purpose of this CAREER proposal is to apply a novel information flow optimization technique, termed Optimal Information Flow (OIF) synthesis, to address a few selected, yet representative, technological challenges in each of the three areas identified above. The key enabler, as well as the uniqueness, of the proposed approach is the novel use of directed information, an information-theoretic quantity that allows for the identification and prioritization of task-relevant information flow over the network. Our starting point is the zero-delay rate-distortion theory and its successful applications to single-channel NCSs. To address (1), we apply directed information to develop a real-time, task-dependent data compression algorithm for high-volume data streams. Our target applications include cloud-based visual servoing for autonomous driving, where we study the extent that data-rate reduction from video streams is possible without deteriorating control performance. To tackle (2), we pursue new approaches to multi-channel NCS design by blending the existing NCS theory with network information theory. We will demonstrate that an appropriate control-communication co-design effectively reduces fuel consumption of autonomous vehicle platoons. For (3), we will study both cryptographic and non-cryptographic privacy preserving mechanisms for cloud-based control systems. We propose design principles for achieving the optimal utility-privacy balance based on the OIF synthesis. Instead of carrying out these three research tasks in a domain-specific manner, we emphasize the underlying roles of directed information in each task, thereby contributing to the well-recognized academic challenge of integrating control theory with information theory. This CAREER proposal also involves innovative educational activities, including the development of a unique graduate-level curriculum on NCSs, in order to maximize the synergistic effects between research and education.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern society is becoming increasingly automated. From fleets of self-driving cars to swarms of satellites orbiting the Earth, many of today’s technologies rely on networks of sensors, computers, and controllers that constantly exchange information to make decisions. These are called networked control systems (NCSs), and they represent the backbone of modern autonomy. While they promise great benefits for safety, efficiency, and convenience, they also face significant challenges. The rise of “Big Data” has created overwhelming demands for bandwidth. Multiple agents competing for limited communication channels make coordination difficult. At the same time, transmitting sensitive data raises concerns about privacy and vulnerability to cyberattacks.

This NSF-supported research project addressed these issues through an idea called Optimal Information Flow (OIF). At the heart of OIF is a concept from information theory known as directed information, which measures not just correlation but also causation, and quantifies how useful the information is for decision-making. By focusing on the information that truly matters for control, OIF helps design communication strategies that make better use of network resources. Throughout the project, this idea was applied to problems involving massive data streams, multi-user coordination, and privacy in cloud-based control.

The first area of exploration was the challenge of Big Data. Consider an autonomous car streaming video to a cloud server for real-time navigation. Sending every frame in full detail would overwhelm any network. To address this, we developed new methods of compressing data that preserve only what is essential for control. This led to the Simultaneous Perception and Action Design (SPADE) algorithm, which determines both how sensors should collect data and how controllers should act on it in real time. The work also extended to continuous-time systems, prompting a new view of how sensors transmit information. Instead of sending fixed batches of data at regular intervals, sensors could operate in an event-based way, reporting only when something important changes. This was applied to neuromorphic vision sensors, or event cameras, which mimic how the human eye reacts to motion. By combining these sensors with OIF-based compression theory, we showed how robots and autonomous systems could navigate more efficiently using less communication bandwidth.

The second thrust of research addressed the coordination of multiple agents sharing limited communication resources. A useful example is a platoon of autonomous trucks traveling in formation. Each vehicle must constantly share information to maintain efficiency and safety. However, unrestricted communication would overload the network. To prevent this, optimization algorithms were developed to allocate communication resources among sensors in the most effective way. These algorithms accounted for limited bandwidth and sought to maximize system performance. On the theoretical side, we showed that the concept of conditional directed information can be applied to understand the fundamental limits of what such multi-agent NCSs can achieve. While many questions remain, these advances provide a stepping stone toward large-scale networks that operate smoothly even under tight communication constraints.

The third theme of the project was privacy and security. As more control systems move to the cloud, the risk of exposing sensitive data grows. Location signals, health information, or even energy usage patterns can all reveal details about individuals or organizations. Malicious actors can also disrupt networks by injecting false data. To guard against these risks, we developed methods to secure NCSs using cryptographic techniques such as homomorphic encryption, which allows data to remain encrypted while being processed, and secure multiparty computation, which lets different parties collaborate without revealing their private data. These methods were tested in contexts ranging from secure reinforcement learning to spacecraft coordination, where multiple satellites must plan collision-avoiding maneuvers without exposing proprietary orbital data. We also introduced an information-theoretic measure of risk to quantify the vulnerability of a system to false data injection attacks, providing a new tool for designing resilient architectures.

This project was accompanied by significant educational activity. A new graduate-level course on networked control systems was created and taught repeatedly at the University of Texas at Austin, bringing the latest research directly into the classroom. Undergraduate students were also engaged through Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), contributing to projects on vision-based control with compressed data. In total, the project produced 15 journal publications and 13 conference papers, ensuring wide dissemination of results to both the scientific community and the engineering field.

In conclusion, the project demonstrated how information theory can guide the design of next-generation control systems. By identifying and prioritizing task-relevant information, the work provides a pathway toward systems that are more efficient in handling large data streams, more effective in coordinating multiple agents, and more secure against threats to privacy and integrity. The implications extend across domains: vehicles that consume less fuel, robots that perceive the world with greater efficiency, and satellites that maneuver safely while protecting sensitive data.

abstractText:
Many primate species are partially or completely arboreal, able to move adeptly over narrow, steep, and bending branches in trees. In this project, investigators will expand their research on the mechanics of walking and leaping in wild primates moving in their natural environments, to provide a deeper understanding of primate arboreality. The team will use advanced and durable video technologies that permit high-resolution measures of locomotion in the wild. The results of this project will further our understanding of locomotor adaptations that are thought to be central to the evolution of our early primate ancestors. The project will support undergraduate and graduate student training and will enhance K-12 STEM education and public outreach through high school programs and collaborations with established science outreach programs at UT Austin. Findings from this project will be relevant to primate conservation efforts, science education, and community outreach at the field locations. 

This project will test hypotheses about the proximate and ultimate determinants of primate locomotor adaptation through analysis of fifteen species of free-ranging strepsirrhines and cercopithecoids. The project expands upon the investigators' previous analysis of quadrupedalism among platyrrhines and includes a three-dimensional kinematic analysis of arboreal leaping. The investigators will document locomotor kinematics of primates moving in their natural habitats using multi-camera, high-speed, high-resolution videography, sampling arboreal locomotion on a range of substrates and quantifying standard kinematic spatiotemporal variables. The morphology of the arboreal locomotor substrates will be quantified using novel remote sensing methods, with specific measurements including substrate diameter, orientation, height above the ground, and compliance. By expanding the sampled range of locomotor behaviors, body sizes, substrates, and taxa, this project will facilitate a more comprehensive investigation of how substrate variation and phylogenetic history have influenced primate locomotor adaptation and evolution. Such knowledge is critical to understanding the adaptive context in which the distinctive aspects of primate locomotion evolved.

projectOutComesReport:
The majority of primate species are partially or completely tree-dwelling (arboreal), and they often captivate observers with their ability to move with ease over narrow, steep, and bending branches. The goal of this project was to investigate the mechanics of walking and leaping in wild primates moving in their natural environments, to provide a deeper understanding of primate arboreal athleticism. Past studies of primate locomotor mechanics have largely come from laboratory-based research, but in this research we used advanced and durable video technologies that permit high-resolution measures of locomotion in the wild. Our results will further our understanding of locomotor adaptations that are thought to be central to the evolution of our early primate ancestors.

Project research was first designed to test hypotheses about primate locomotor adaptation through analysis of eight species of  free-ranging strepsirrhines in Ranomafana National Park and Anja Community Reserve, Madagascar (Eulemur rubriventer, Eulemur rufifrons, Hapalemur aureus, Hapalemur griseus, Lemur catta, Prolemur simus, Propithecus edwardsi, and Varecia variegata) and eight species of free-ranging cercopithecoids in Kibale National Park, Uganda (Allochrocebus lhoesti, Cercopithecus ascanius, Cercopithecus mitis, Chlorocebus aethiops, Colobus guereza, Lophocebus albigena, Papio anubis, and Piliocolobus tephrosceles). This research expands on our similar investigation of quadrupedal locomotion in eleven species of free-ranging platyrrhines at field sites in Costa Rica and Ecuador, resulting in a combined dataset on quadrupedalism for 27 primate species distributed across the extant radiation. This work represents an unprecedented dataset for the quantitative analysis of primate gait variability and its determinants in free-ranging primates moving in their natural environments. Though analyses are still ongoing, existing results support several general conclusions. Fundamentally, our field data generally corroborate laboratory studies of primate gait and locomotion, but capture additional aspects of locomotor variability and flexibility in response to the complexity of natural environments. For instance, we found evidence that lemurs adjusted some gait parameters based on their height in the canopy, suggesting that the risk of injury from falling may be an additional influence on primate gait that has – as of yet – received little attention (perhaps at least partly due to the difficulty of modeling this parameter in laboratory environments). Overall, our results suggest that primate gait patterns are not exclusively tailored to “precarious” supports (i.e., narrow or oblique substrates) but are used across a variety of supports. For example, in an analysis of limb joint postures in 14 species from our wild primate dataset (five platyrrhines, five cercopithecoids, and four lemurs) we found that joint postures changed very little in response to changing substrate parameters, though - as previously shown in laboratory studies - substrate orientation exerted a stronger influence than substrate diameter or compliance per se. Overall, our results routinely demonstrate significant differences in quadrupedal locomotor patterns among major taxonomic groups of primates - independent of any influence of substrate parameters on locomotion - suggesting that evolutionary history may be a better predictor of gait than substrate diameter or orientation.

Second, project research also included new quantitative analyses of arboreal leaping in wild primates, and - as in our analyses of quadrupedal locomotion - how the natural variability of the arboreal environment impacts leaping performance. Curiously, we found that in some cases the compliance (i.e., “bendiness”) of arboreal supports can actually enhance leaping performance in wild colobus monkeys., showing that the monkeys actively pump branches before leaping, augmenting their vertical velocity at leaping take-off, and harness the swaying motions of tree trunks to cross large gaps, augmenting horizontal velocity at take-off. This deliberate branch manipulation to produce a mechanical effect for stronger propulsion fits into the framework of instrumental problem-solving, and suggests a high level of cognitive involvement during primate arboreal locomotion. Additionally, to facilitate project research, we developed a standardized protocol for the three-dimensional analysis of primate leaping under wild conditions that could be adopted to quantitatively study the locomotor biomechanics of other animals moving in wild, free-ranging environments.  Overall, our results highlight the utility of the techniques newly developed for this research to promote understanding of both the proximate environmental and broader evolutionary determinants of primate locomotion.

This project has resulted in five peer-reviewed publications, and 13 professional conference presentations. At the University of Texas at Austin, it has provided training and mentorship for a graduate student and four undergraduate students. The UT PI and research team disseminated project research to K-12 students from underrepresented groups via UT Austin's Environmental Science Institute's "Hot Science Cool Talks" lecture series and to undergraduate students via involvement in the Undergraduate Research Workshop sponsored by UT Austin's Senate of College Councils. At NEOMED, project funds supported the training of a postdoctoral research fellow, a graduate student, four undergraduate students, and two high school students. The NEOMED PI taught three short courses on primate biodiversity and biomechanics at a local STEM high school affiliated with the university.

abstractText:
Deep neural networks have emerged as a transformative computing technology in the last few years. However, as illustrated by recent research on adversarial machine learning,  they can behave in obviously erroneous ways on anomalous or adversarial inputs and cannot be debugged using traditional software development methods.  Thus, there is an urgent need for developing formal methods techniques that can assure the safety of neural networks, particularly in safety- or security-critical application domains. Motivated by this problem, this project investigates automated formal reasoning techniques for provably safe deep learning. 

In particular, the investigators explore verification methods for certifying robustness properties of trained networks as well as new verified training methods for finding network parameters that are safe by construction.  The technical approach closely couples techniques for automated formal reasoning about systems (in particular abstraction) and continuous optimization. In particular, the project explores the use of automated abstraction techniques, originally developed for reasoning about human-written programs, in the analysis of neural networks. The project investigates the coupling of abstraction and gradient-based optimization in searching for correctness proofs and network parameters. The project introduces undergraduate and high school students from underrepresented groups to research on programming languages and formal methods through outreach programs centered around the topics on artificial intelligence.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The intellectual outcomes of the project are as follows.

 

  • We developed a new technique, and a system called Charon that implements the technique, for formally verifying adversarial robustness properties of neural networks. The method improved upon the state-of-the-art of neural network verification via a new abstraction-refinement technique. The 2019 paper describing the method was selected as a Distinguished Paper at the prestigious PLDI conference. The paper has gone on to have 100+ citations. 

  • We introduced a new form of reinforcement learning (RL) in which every exploration step is provably correct. The approach, called Revel, was based on a mirror descent algorithm in which gradient-based updates alternate with verified program synthesis steps. A paper on this topic was published at NeurIPS 2020. The paper has gone on to have 100+ citations. 


  • We also obtained strong results for the problem of learning worst-case-safe parameters for programs that use neural networks as well as symbolic, human-written code. We published a paper on this topic at the ICLR 2022 conference. 


  • We developed a framework, called Spice, for safe reinforcement learning in the presence of blackbox environment models. A paper on this topic was published at the ICLR 2023 conference.

  • We also developed a reinforcement learning (RL) framework in which the learned policy comes with a machine-checkable certificate of provable adversarial robustness.A paper on this topic was published at the SatML 2024 conference.

  • We developed a novel approach to learning provably safe network congestion control algorithms. The method follows  first to connect learning-abled software systems A paper on this topic is currently under review. 



The broader impacts of the project are as follows. 


  • The project has developed novel approaches to reliable AI that can have impact in a wide range of societally relevant applications.

  • Resources from the project were used to train several graduate and undergraduate students. Two of the graduate students supported by the project, Abinav Verma and Greg Anderson, graduated and embarked on tenure-track faculty positions.

  • Research results from the project have been integrated into the PIs' undergraduate and graduate courses on trustworthy AI and formal methods.

  • The PIs have given several public talks on research results from the project, including in a tutorial at the prestigious POPL 2023 conference.

abstractText:
This project will study ways to improve classroom instruction grounded in science practices to address inequities in science education for emerging bilingual students. Currently, many elementary school teachers are unfamiliar with science practices and are unprepared to teach emerging bilingual students since they never received training in either area. This project will address this lack of training and create research-based resources for teacher educators that focus on developing preservice elementary teachers’ understanding and abilities to support emerging bilingual students’ engagement in science practices. The study will be guided by the following objectives, which are to research: (1) the understandings of exemplary elementary teachers around science, language, and emerging bilingual students, and the relationship between these understandings and their instructional practices for supporting student sensemaking; (2) preservice teachers’ understandings and practices related to supporting emerging bilingual students’ sensemaking; (3) the development of an elementary science methods course, and educator resources, that support teacher learning about the role of language in science practices and approaches for supporting emerging bilingual students’ sensemaking; and (4) the impact of this course, and its teacher educator resources, on preservice teachers’ understandings and instructional practices. With little prior research having looked at the intersection of science and language learning, this project will advance knowledge in this regard.

Through a mixed-methods design, this project will investigate interrelated aspects of teacher understandings, teacher practice, and teacher learning around supporting emerging bilingual students’ scientific sensemaking. Phase 1 of the project includes examining the instructional approaches around science practices of exemplary elementary school teachers that work in different types of school contexts with emerging bilingual students. Such strategies will go beyond traditional subject-matter knowledge and skills to include teacher encouragement of students using linguistic and nonlinguistic modes for communicating ideas; development of a deeper understanding of natural scientific phenomena; and engagement with and valuing of students’ families, communities, and lived experiences. These combined efforts will capture and illustrate compelling examples of possible instantiations of engagement in science practices while being mindful of and responsive to emerging bilingual students’ language assets, needs, and English development. Findings from Phase 1 will be used for Phase 2 of this project, which focuses on iteratively designing and analyzing a science methods course and resources for preservice teachers’ pedagogical development across science and language learning.

The CAREER program is a National Science Foundation (NSF)-wide activity that offers awards in support of junior faculty who exemplify the role of teacher-scholars through outstanding research, excellent education, and the integration of education and research within the context of the mission of their organizations. This project is supported by NSF's Discovery Research PreK-12 (DRK-12) program. DRK-12 seeks to significantly enhance the learning and teaching of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) by preK-12 students and teachers through research and development of innovative resources, models and tools. Projects in the DRK-12 program build on fundamental research in STEM education and prior research and development efforts that provide theoretical and empirical justification for proposed projects.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
This Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) grant will pioneer a novel three-dimensional nanolithography system using light interactions with colloidal nanoparticles. The ability to create a three-dimensional object at the nanoscale has enabled unique material properties and device performances. However, almost all of the existing lithography systems are based on complicated mechanical, electronic, and optical hardware that can be prohibitively expensive. This award supports fundamental research to provide the required knowledge for three-dimensional nanolithography that is based solely on colloid-light interactions instead of current expensive lithography, hence nanolithography with inexpensive hardware. The new process focuses on colloidal nanoparticles, which will serve as elementary building blocks that can manipulate and shape light for nanoscale patterning. This system will enable scalable printing of complex three-dimensional nanostructures for needleless drug delivery, multifunctional materials, and stretchable sensors. The results of this research will find broad application in biomedical, energy, electronic, and aerospace industries that will benefit the U.S. economy and the advance its manufacturing sector. This research is interdisciplinary and will further understandings in nanotechnology, physics, materials science, and engineering. The integrated research and educational goals will greatly increase engineering education in society through direct engagement of K-12 students, teachers, parents, and the local community in nanotechnology and nanomanufacturing. 

This research aims to overcome the key barriers to existing 3D nanolithography systems, which can have high operating cost, limited patterning resolution, and/or low fabrication throughput. State-of-the-art direct-write approaches, such as electron-beam, focused-ion-beam, two-photon lithography, can achieve fine features and have played critical roles in laboratory device demonstrations. However, these systems require serial patterning and layer-by-layer processes that are time intensive and difficult to scale. This research diverges from the traditional hardware-intensive approaches to lithography, and replaces them with colloidal nanoparticles that are illuminated to generate a wealth of near-field optical nanopatterns. By tailoring the light properties and particle parameters, such interactions will be harnessed as a novel mechanism to pattern complex 3D geometries. This approach combines the cost-effectiveness of "bottom-up" self-assembly, while retaining the user-specified pattern controllability of "top-down" lithography. The research team will perform rigorous modeling of near-field light-particle interactions to investigate the image formation mechanism, develop fabrication processes to control structure geometry and material composition, mitigate process defects and increase yield in a scale-up prototype system, and demonstrate continuous printing of complex 3D nanostructures into novel functional devices.

projectOutComesReport:
This project focused on pioneering a novel three-dimensional (3D) nanolithography system using light interactions with colloidal nanoparticles. The ability to create 3D objects at the nanoscale has enabled unique material properties and device performances. However, almost all of the existing lithography approaches have a tradeoff between pattern resolution and scalability, making high-throughput nanopatterning a significant challenge. This project investigated fundamental research to provide the required knowledge for 3D nanolithography that is based solely on colloid-light interactions. Instead of complex mechanical, electronic, and optical hardware that can be prohibitively expensive, this new process utilizes colloidal nanoparticles, as elementary building blocks that can manipulate and shape light for nanoscale patterning. By tailoring the light properties and particle parameters, such interactions will be harnessed as a novel mechanism to pattern complex 3D geometries. The results of this research will find broad application in energy, electronic, and aerospace industries that will benefit the U.S. economy and the advance its manufacturing sector. The integrated research and outreach goals have greatly increased engineering education in nanotechnology and nanomanufacturing through direct engagements of K-12 students, teachers, parents, and science museums in the local community. 

This project has led to key developments at the intersection of nanotechnology, physics, materials science, and engineering. The overarching goal of this research is demonstrating is that colloidal particles in various geometric assembles can be used to pattern complex 3D nanostructures and has been theoretically and experimentally demonstrated. This research has developed rigorous optical models to examine near-field light-particle interactions and better understand the image formation mechanism, enabling the precise control of the pattern geometry. To create 3D geometry beyond polymer materials, this project has also developed and demonstrated multilayer fabrication processes to control structure geometry and material composition. The patterning techniques developed in this research have led to several novel nanostructures with physical properties that cannot be found in traditional macroscale materials. These properties include highly porous material with near-unity refractive index, low density, and high stiffness, transparent conductors that are mechanically stretchable, and dynamic iridescent surface that can change color in real time. The novel colloidal patterning mechanism was harnessed to build a roll-to-roll prototype system that can continuously print 3D periodic nanostructures on flexible substrates with high throughput. This system was coupled with automated inspection protocols to mitigate process defects and increase yield, demonstrating that the light interactions with colloidal particles can be a scalable, high-throughput method for nanopatterning.

abstractText:
The Hikurangi subduction zone offshore the eastern North Island of New Zealand has characteristics that provide a globally unique window into a fundamental aspect of how stress builds up and is relieved as an oceanic plate thrusts (or ?subducts?) beneath continental crust. Recently, seismologists have recognized that subduction megathrust faults undergo slip in episodic ?slow slip events?. Prior to the discovery of slow slip events in the last decade, our paradigms of fault slip were focused on seismic slip in major earthquakes. Since the discovery of slow slip, most studies have focused on deep (>20-40 km depth) slow slip events, but we now realize that shallow slow slip events (<5-15 km depth) exist that are much more accessible to near-source investigations. These shallow slow fault slip events are centered beneath the ocean so onshore instruments have not been able to measure how much surface deformation occurs. This study takes advantage of planned International Ocean Discovery Program drilling to install sensors in two boreholes that will measure properties indicative of change in the shallow crust that the episodic fault activity causes.  Senior researchers in borehole instrumentation will mentor mid-early career scientists, passing along extensive knowledge of such complex implementation and research. Japanese, New Zealand, and German collaborators will participate with the US investigators in this international study, and local communities will benefit from scientist outreach associated with cruises off New Zealand. This study is being undertaken as a ?community proposal?, whereby all data will be immediately publicly available.
 
The shallowest, well-documented slow slip events on Earth occur at the northern Hikurangi margin, offshore Gisborne, New Zealand, at <5-15 km depth. They recur approximately every 1-2 years, with slip on the plate boundary interface of up to 15-20 cm. The unusually close proximity of the Gisborne slow slip events to the seafloor, the large slow slip event magnitudes (equivalent to an earthquake magnitude Mw ~6.3-6.8), and short recurrence intervals makes this the ideal setting for evaluating the near-source hydrological, geochemical, and thermal response of the offshore subduction margin to large, frequent, well-documented deformation transients. The borehole observatory data will clarify the role that fluid pressures, fluid flow, and temperature play in the occurrence of slow slip events, as well as the influence of slow slip event deformation on fluid and geochemical cycling within the forearc. This project will establish the borehole facility and set-up open data access. Analysis of the first two years of data, recovered by ROV, will evaluate the deformation, hydrological, and geochemical responses near the source of slow slip, as well as document the thermal regime of shallow slow slip. One of the borehole installations will target the region surrounding the shallow portion of the megathrust fault , while sensors in a second borehole will target the over-riding plate ~5 km above the slow slip event source.

projectOutComesReport:
Subduction zone plate boundaries produce the world's largest and deadliest earthquakes and tsunamis, but we know little about when they will strike because most subduction zone earthquakes occur miles beneath the ocean floor, making these faults difficult to monitor using conventional land-based methods. This project aimed to design, construct, and install a suite of novel sensors into two boreholes drilled beneath deep water and into the Earth's crust offshore of Northern New Zealand. This region is of particular interest because it is the site of frequent "slow slip events", a type of slow motion earthquake that involves centimeters to tens of centimeters of movement along the subduction zone fault over days to years. In some cases, these slow motion earthquakes can precede (and possibly trigger) major earthquake ruptures, such as was observed prior to the magnigtude 9 Tohoku earthquake offshore Japan in 2011. The observation of these enigmatic slow slip events also provides a new window into the physics of earthquake-generating faults.  

The sensors and samplng systems developed in this project were successfully installed, within only a few hundred meters to a few km of the source regions of earthquakes and slow slip events. as part of Integrated Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 375 in 2018. The observatory systems include: (1) pressure sensors that monitor the accumulation and release of strain caused by tectonic motion and fault and earthquake slip; (2) temperature sensors to monitor changes in fluid movement and heat transfer that may be associated with fault motions; and (3) chemical sampling devices to provide a record of variations in fluid movement and composition that may also be associated with fault slip.

In 2019 and again in 2021, visits to the boreholes using a remotely operated submersible successfully accessed these observatory systems, and acquired long-term records of pressure in the subsurface. These initial data document a large slow slip event in 2019, and provide observations both at high resolution and in the offshore-most reaches of the subduction fault close to its shallow edge at the ocean trench. The new data provide insight into fault motion in unprecedented detail, including the migration of fault slip as the event unfolded, and the observation of multiple smaller slip events far offshore that went undetected by other (land-based) sensor networks. The fluid sampling system and temperature sensors remain in place, and will be recovered, along with data and samples, in the coming years. The pressure data obtained to date provide key new insights into the accumulation and release of stress in the shallowest subduction zone, with key implications for hazards posed by tsunami and shallow earthquake slip.

abstractText:
This Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) Program grant will develop the fundamental science for the design and characterization a new family of damage-tolerant composite materials that are strong, stiff, and ductile. Carbon fiber reinforced polymer-matrix composites are currently considered state-of-the-art for defense, energy, and transportation applications. These polymer-matrix composites, however, suffer several limitations, including brittle fracture and poor damage tolerance, both of which result in catastrophic failures in composite structures. The novel composites, based on graphene within a carbon fiber matrix, address major shortcomings of traditional polymer-matrix alternatives such as the lack of ductility and the propensity to damage and therefore has the potential to help save billions of dollars in failure and inspection costs across multiple industries on an annual basis. The polymer-free nature of the graphene-carbon fiber (matrix) composite will enable resistance to high impact energy, electromagnetic interference (EMI), high temperatures, and harsh environments. These multifunctional aspects will significantly reduce cost and design complexity and can potentially result in the manufacturing of safer and more durable structures for defense, energy, and transportation applications. This project will also result in effective platforms to attract and train students in this emerging field and has the increasing enrollment in Mechanical Engineering at the University of New Mexico, specifically women. The grant also supports activities directed at increasing the interest in STEM education in the local community among ethnic minorities including Native American college students and Hispanic K-12 students.

This project will investigate and elucidate the underlying mechanisms that can be used to control and tailor the ductility and damage progression in carbonaceous nanocomposites, specifically in graphene-carbon fiber composites. Graphene-based materials have been extensively studied recently, mainly by incorporating trial and error approaches, to optimize their mechanical properties rather than effectively studying to understand the underlying mechanisms. These studies have shown promising results but cannot be used to tailor mechanical properties due to the vast design parameter space available to graphene-based materials. This project utilizes a combined numerical modeling and state-of-the-art multi-scale characterization approach to understand and tailor mechanical properties in the graphene-carbon fiber (matrix) composites. The research objectives include the understanding of the stress-transfer mechanisms at the graphene-carbon fiber interface and elucidation of the underlying failure mechanisms in these composites. These resolution of these underlying mechanisms will answer some of the long-standing scientific questions and challenges regarding the strength-ductility trade-off in nanocomposites.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
The physical processes dictating the spectrum of fault slip modes (spanning destructive earthquakes
to slow slip events and aseismic creep) and the links between these behaviors and long-term
morphotectonic evolution of subduction systems are not understood. There is a fundamental
need to address this important problem with an integrated, system-level approach combining
geodynamical modeling with high-quality geophysical and geological constraints on subduction
margin characteristics.

This project will conduct an interdisciplinary, multinational collaborative program involving the USA, New Zealand, Japan and the UK to evaluate system-level controls on processes that govern both slip behavior and long-term deformation at subduction zones. The focus is on the Hikurangi margin in New Zealand, where GPS data show a transition in slip behavior from predominantly stick-slip
in the south to aseismic creep in the northern North Island, and where a wide range of subduction-related
processes and characteristics vary along-strike. The aim is to rigorously investigate the feedbacks
between plate interface slip behavior, solid and fluid mass fluxes, and manifestations of plate boundary mechanics in the long-term geological record that likely reflect common driving processes linking forearc uplift, sediment transfer and underplating, plate boundary strength, and seismogenesis. The Principal Investigators will address this important problem through an integrated approach combining large-scale seismic imaging, paleoseismology, and geomorphology, focused through the lens of state-of-the-art numerical modelling.

projectOutComesReport:
This project aimed to deepen our understanding of earthquake behavior on sunbduction zone plate boundaries - locations where one of Earth's tectonic plates "dives" beneath another. The fault zones formed at these plate boundaries, termed "megathrusts", are responsible for many of the planet's largest, most energetic, and damaging earthquakes and tsunamis. However, detailed information about these plate boundasries, and particuarly about why some megathrusts appear to store energy and slip in damaging earthquakes, whereas others move more slowly by creeping continuously or in slow slip events, a form of slow-motion and non-damaging earthquake that unfolds over days to weeks to even months (inseat of seconds to minutes), remains elusive. The Hikurangi subduction zone, located offshore of Northern New Zealand, was chosen for this project because it exhibits a clear change along ots length, from creeping behavior in the North, to locking and stress buildup in the South.

This project was designed to combine detailed imaging of the megathrust and surrounding rock with sophisticated computer models of plate movement and stressing of the rock and sediment in the region, in order to test some of the leading ideas about factors that control slow slip events and creeping megathrust behavior. Using computer simulations of the system, we found that geometric roughness - for example, the presence of seamounts - on the subducting plate play a key role in explaining patterns of earthquakes and slip: the areas in front of seamounts are subjected to extra stresses, and are more prone to regular (fast) earthquakes. In contrast, areas behind these features lie in a "stress shadow" and should be more prone to creeping and slow slip. The modeling and imaging, taken together, also suggest an important role of fluids in promoting slow slip. These fluids are carried in thick sedimentary deposits atop the subducting plate, and thus are delivered to the slow slip source zone deeper along the megathrust. Our results show that these fluids are surprisingly abundant, and that their release may correlate with the patches of the megathrust where slow slip events initiate.

PI Name: Darrell Velegol
Proposal Number: 1705278

Membrane technologies, especially reverse osmosis (RO), are now at the forefront of water purification from lower-quality water sources such as seawater, brackish water, and wastewater.  The objective of this project is to minimize membrane fouling by producing oxygen at the membrane surface to impede the growth of biofilms on the membrane.  Biofouling has the largest negative impact on desalination membrane performance.  This fundamental research has the potential to transform membrane performance by significantly decreasing the energy use of membranes and increasing their usable lifetime.  The fundamental principles learned are anticipated to lead to solutions that are scalable and commercially viable and can improve municipal and industrial water treatment to help meet the growing national demand for potable water.

Numerous efforts have focused on improving RO efficiency by pretreatment, minimizing concentration polarization (CP), and mitigating fouling.  Current methods have not overcome the problem in a feasible manner, especially for concentration polarization; however, no study has been reported on the application of microbubbles generated in situ to disturb the CP boundary layer.  The hypothesis is that catalytically generating microbubbles at a membrane surface will produce localized micromixing, which will significantly reduce both concentration polarization and particle-bacteria-organic fouling.  To test the overall hypothesis and meet the objective, three important fundamental questions must be answered, and form the intellectual merit of this research:  1) What is the rate of microbubble formation, and the microbubble size distribution, given a particular catalyst type, catalyst loading fraction, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) dosing profile, and local pressure (i.e., must exceed Henry's law solubility)? 2) For a given microbubble production rate and size distribution, what is the increase in water effluent due to the different mechanisms of micromixing for concentration polarization, and liftoff for membrane fouling species? and 3) For a given microbubble production rate, what is the disinfection capacity for biofilm-forming microorganisms using the produced oxidant (reactive oxygen species), at production levels that avoid membrane damage?  The approach is to incorporate catalysts in the membrane module (either membrane surface or spacers), and then during the operation of the membrane, to inject pulses of H2O2 or other reactants that will produce microbubbles at the membrane surface.  A primary figure of merit for this work is an increased water flux through the membrane over time.  The broader impacts of this proposal focus on educating Ph.D. students (including internships with Dow Chemical, our NSF GOALI partner) and undergrads, as well as technological commercialization (with partner Dow Chemical).  Producing microbubbles and generating localized micromixing could be achieved at commercial scale.  Ph.D. and undergrad education as well as internships and entrepreneurship training will form part of the student experience.

projectOutComesReport:
The overall goal of this project was to develop methods to solve the two most common problems in operation of desalination membranes that are used for brackish and sea water purification as well as for wastewater recycling. These challenges include membrane fouling by organic and inorganic materials and transient accumulation of dissolved solutes (such as salt) on the membrane surface that leads to decreasing in driving force for transport, known as concentration polarization. The central hypothesis driving this project was that that catalytically generating microbubbles at a membrane surface will produce localized micromixing, which will significantly reduce both concentration polarization and membrane fouling.

 

Intellectual Merit. 

We were able to demonstrate the catalytic nanoparticles deposited on commercial reverse osmosis causes degradation of the common chemical hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen. The oxygen bubbles released at a high rate during this process causes enhanced mixing near the membrane surface was found to be sufficient to almost completely eliminate concentration polarization and prevent various kinds of fouling including colloidal, bacterial and silica fouling. We were also able to show that commercial nanoparticles can be coated by spray coating on commercial RO membranes in order to provide a path to scale up this process. 3 peer review publications and one patent resulted as a result of this work and two other publications are in progress.

 

Broader Impacts.

In this work we collaborated with Dow/Dupont Water Solutions to develop a scalable technique to make water purification more sustainable and efficient. During the project, one graduate student interned with Dupont for 6 months and three graduate students and one undergraduate student was trained. The project also provided the project team opportunities to participate in outreach activities including running 1-week long Science camp (Water Heroes) with Penn State Science U and as a part of the University of Texas Girl Day activities (that impacts over 6000 K-12 students every year).

abstractText:
A common task in statistics is prediction; for example, a practitioner may be interested in predicting the presence of a disease given genetic information about an individual. Due to recent advances in data collection, frequently one has access to datasets which contain a massive number of predictors, but with correspondingly few subjects. This setting is generally referred to as the "big P, small n" scenario. Drawing meaningful conclusions under such circumstances is generally impossible unless the underlying data satisfy certain structural assumptions. The simplest such structural assumption is that only a small number of the predictors are relevant; in this setting, finding the useful predictors corresponds to finding a so-called "needle in a haystack." The goal of this project is to construct procedures which adapt to this, and other, structural assumptions. The project will focus on methods based on decision trees, which are flowchart-like structures in which predictions are based on whether the predictors satisfy various rules. Usually an ensemble of decision trees are constructed, with the predictions for each individual tree averaged. While decision tree ensembles are frequently used with high dimensional data, it is unclear to what extent they adapt to the structural properties of the data. This project will show that, in practice, off-the-shelf decision tree ensembling methods do not adapt to common structural assumptions, and will develop new methods which do. In addition to developing methods with strong theoretical support, this project will support the development of an R package to give practitioners easy access to our methodology.

    
The PI will develop Bayesian methods for incorporating structural information into tree-based ensemble methods, and establish theoretically the benefit of making use of this additional information. This forms a nonparametric counterpart to the parametric approaches used in linear models, such as the lasso, graphical lasso, or group lasso; Bayesian approaches in the parametric setting include the use of variable selection priors, such as spike-and-slab priors and global-local shrinkage priors. Structural information will be incorporated by modifying the commonly used priors on decision tree ensembles so that the prior is concentrated on models which satisfy the desired structure. The PI will first investigate the theoretical properties of a sparsity inducing prior which is designed to eliminate unnecessary predictors. Sparsity here is obtained by applying a sparsity inducing Dirichlet prior to the a priori probability that a given branch is associated to a given predictor. This prior will be extended to allow for grouped variable selection in a similar manner to the group lassoby considering the class of Dirichlet tree priors, and further to accommodate graphical structures in the predictors through sparsity inducing logistic normal priors. Additionally, the PI will develop computationally efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms to fit the resulting models. Compared to existing methods, these structural priors will be shown to lead to substantial gains in predictive accuracy, and to more accurate scientific discovery.

projectOutComesReport:
This project had the aim of designing machine learning tools based on decision trees which are capable of detecting and adapting to structural information (such as whether genes lie in the same genetic pathway, or whether a large number of predictor variables are irrelevant).

This project largely succeeded in addressing all of the goals of the proposal. We successfully provided a mathematically sound theoretical basis for the techniques we developed, and carried out the program of incorporating both grouping information and graphical structure (such as the network structure of a gene regulatory network) into decision tree procedures. Additionally, the grant provided funding for a number of projects beyond the original scope of the grant, including problems in sequential process monitoring, spatial statistics, and causal inference. As of the writing of this report, one project outlined in the grant proposal is yet to be complete (incorporating the insights of Bayesian procedures into decision tree boosting algorithms), but will ideally be completed by the end of 2020.

This grant provided support for 13 publications in statistics journals (8 of which have been accepted), 2 publications in refereed machine learning conferences, and provided PhD dissertation projects for 5 students (2 completed, 3 in progress), of which two are female and one is black. Additionally, projects completed under this grant composed dissertation chapters for two students (both female) who were not advised by the PI.

The methodology developed in the proposal has wide-ranging applications, and we applied the methods to problems in analysis of large-scale medical expenditure datasets, clinical trials, quality control, gene expression data, and large-scale online ratings data. We anticipate the methodology developed will be applied in the future to an ever-expanding set of problems; currently, we are working on projects involving Financial Technology (Fintech) data as well as large publicly collected observational datasets, with the aim of combining our procedures with tools from causal inference. For example, in the Fintech applications, we aim to estimate the effects of various loan policies on the profits of a company.

The methodology developed in this grant has produced accompanying publicly available software, and has also been incorporated into software packages developed by others.

abstractText:
This research project is concerned with important physical phenomena driven by collision and diffusion of particles, whose mathematical description is based on partial differential equations of kinetic type. It is driven by applications in gas dynamics and plasma physics as well by mathematical interests in analysis, partial differential equations and mathematical physics. Kinetic equations are used to describe evolution of interacting particles, such as gas molecules, ions and electrons in a plasma. The most famous kinetic equation is the Boltzmann equation: formulated by Ludwig Boltzmann in 1872, this equation describes motion of a large class of gases. Later, in 1936 Lev Landau derived from the Boltzmann equation a new mathematical model for motion of plasma. This latter equation was named the Landau equation. Despite the fact that many mathematicians and physicists have been working on these equations, many important questions are still unanswered due to their mathematical complexity. The proposed research will fundamentally contribute to this field by bridging the gap between mathematical analysis and physics and enable further mathematical understanding of physical phenomena. The work will be enhanced by collaborations at the national and international levels and will help strengthen inter-institutional ties. The research program will be integrated with educational and outreach activities designed to (i) broaden the students' understanding of different research areas, (ii) provide the students with a modern skill set that is essential for different career paths, and (iii) promote existing connections between local institutions in the DC Metro area and help establish new avenues for collaboration and training of high quality scientific workforce. 

The proposed research will advance the knowledge in global properties of solutions to collisional kinetic mathematical models, improving our understanding of non-linear dynamics, entropy, equilibrium, and regularizing effects. The corresponding equations contain integro-differential operators that are highly nonlinear, singular and with degenerating coefficients. Integro-differential equations of this type have received increased attention recently: well-posedness and regularity theory are being developed since many new applications have emerged, among which conformal geometry, stochastic control and image processing. The project aims at advancing knowledge in the theories of kinetic equations, nonlocal integro-differential operators and degenerate differential operators.

projectOutComesReport:
The main outcomes are:

(1) Research: advance the knowledges in global properties of solutions to several mathematical models constituted by nonlinear partial differential equations. In particular, the PI has contributed to the unified theory for global well-posedness of collisional models in plasma, in particular to the homogeneous Landau equation and related models. The PI has also investigated specific class of partial differential equations that describe bacterial self-organization under the effects of chemotaxis.  A third research area concerns  the study of the global well-posedness of a certain class of non-local porous medium equations, where potential depends non-locally on the density distribution.

 

(2) Research dissemination:  The PI's research findings have been published in 17 papers (published in peer reviews journals), and disseminated in 32 venues, including department seminars, national and international workshops and conferences. 

(3) Mentorship:  The PI has advised 4 graduate students and mentored 2 post-doctoral fellows: 

(i) graduate student Ben Lyons, since Fall 2025. 

(ii) graduate student Francisco Unai Lopez, since Fall 2024.

(iii)  Post-doctoral fellow Dominic Wynter, since Fall 2024.

(iv)  Post-doctoral fellow Rene Cabrera, 2022 - 2025.

(v) graduate student  William Golding (Graduated Summer 2024). Currently Post-doctoral fellow at University of  Chicago. 

 (vi) graduate student  Jingjing Xu (graduated Spring 2022). Research Scientist

 (vii) graduate student Xinyu Zhang (graduated Spring 2021). Data Scientist. 

 

The PI has published 9 papers in collaboration with graduate students and 1 with post-doctoral fellow. 

(4) Enhancement of graduate program in Applied Mathematics  at George Washington University (2016-2019) and at the University of Texas at Austin (2019-2025) . The PI has organized special activities to promote graduate research and expose graduate students to national and international well-known mathematicians. This includes 2 workshops and 2 graduate schools:  

(i) workshop "Nonlinear phenomena in DC" held at George Washington University, Washington DC, April 24, 2018. 

(ii) conference Nonlinear phenomena in Stockholm: kinetic meets dispersive, KTH. Sweden, Nov 19-21 2018.

(ii) joint Graduate Spring School in Analysis and PDEs at UT Austin - Texas State San Marcos, May 13 - 20 2024.

(iii) joint Graduate Summer  School in Analysis and PDEs at UT Austin August 15-19 2022.

 

During the duration of this grant the PI has organized 5 additional conferences and workshops and disseminated her research findings in forms of research talks and tutorials in several national and international conferences, workshops and department seminars.
